Sports.title: Anthony Joshua pays tribute to his two best friends killed in a car crash as he returns to the ring for clash with Kristian Prenga
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua pays tribute to his two best friends killed in a car crash as he returns to the ring for clash with Kristian Prenga

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Anthony Joshua paid tribute to two close friends killed in a car crash in December as he returned to the ring for the first time since the tragedy.

Sina Ghami and Latif 'Latz' Ayodele died while the car they were travelling in struck a truck on a road near Lagos in December. The pair were on holiday with Joshua after he beat Jake Paul in Miami.

The heavyweight boxer, who was also in the vehicle, was taken to hospital before being discharged and flying home to the UK - where he attended the funerals of his strength and conditioning coach Ghami and Ayodele, one of his trainers.

Returning to the ring after seven months of inactivity, Joshua beat Albanian Kristian Prenga by knockout in the second round - despite being knocked down twice himself in the first.

Fighting in honour of Ghami and Ayodele, Joshua paid tribute to his friends by having their names printed on his military camouflage trunks.

He also walked to the ring wearing a military-style jacket to match his camo shorts. The jacket featured a medal bar displaying the IBF, IBO, WBA, and WBO titles - which he previously held - alongside pennants bearing Ghami and Ayodele's names.

Meanwhile, ‘Latz x Sina, My Brother's Keeper, MBK’ was printed on the canvas in his corner.

Anthony Joshua wears jacket featuring medal bar with 'Sina' and 'Latz' pennants

Joshua's friends were honoured by having their names printed on the canvas

Asked about how he has been coping after beating Prenga, Joshua said: 'It's been tough,' before becoming emotional. 'That's my brothers. I don't want to talk about that.'

Speaking on DAZN, Matchroom Boxing chief Eddie Hearn added: 'Nobody can imagine what he's been through in that last seven months. In that first round, I thought we'd come back too soon.

'Boxing got him through. To even be in the ring tonight is astonishing. You don't know what he's been through. He had to go to the depths one more time to get up, like he has done the last seven months.'

In February, Joshua memorialised Ghami and Ayodele by having their names tattooed on his arm.

Oleksandr Usyk was ringside for the clash in Jeddah to support Joshua, whom he beat twice in world title fights. Usyk has been working closely with Joshua, supporting his training camp.

Victory for Joshua means he is on track to finally fight Tyson Fury in a long-awaited British heavyweight showdown.

Sports.title: Defensive signings are a MUST after Joe Gomez injury, young star who took his chance and forgotten man Federico Chiesa gives Andoni Iraola food for thought: THINGS WE LEARNED as Liverpool beat Sunderland
Sports.content:
Defensive signings are a MUST after Joe Gomez injury, young star who took his chance and forgotten man Federico Chiesa gives Andoni Iraola food for thought: THINGS WE LEARNED as Liverpool beat Sunderland

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

The Andoni Iraola era got off to a flying start in Nashville with a 4-2 thumping of Sunderland – though the injury to defender Joe Gomez may leave the new Liverpool manager pondering at what cost this win came.

Goals from teenager Kieran Morrison, stand-in captain Dominik Szoboszlai, returning loanee Lewis Koumas and Federico Chiesa helped Iraola to a win and pleasing performance over their fellow Premier League opposition.

But the win was somewhat overshadowed by the first-half injury of Gomez and the fact fellow defender Jeremy Jacquet sat the match out due to a fitness concern of his own. It makes the need for a new defender starkly obvious.

Reds expert Lewis Steele was in the city of cowboy hats, hot chicken wings and honky-tonk bars and brings you his key Tennessee takeaways...

Defensive reinforcements are a necessity

It was the sight that no Reds fan, or the transfer committee, wanted to see.

Just seven minutes into the Iraola era, he had his first injury casualty to deal with. Welcome to Liverpool, some may joke, given the well-documented problems with fitness across the board for the team last season.

Joe Gomez went down off the ball, holding what appeared to be a muscular problem. He had a grimace on his face and a look of resignation. The defender missed the majority of 2024-25 and was in and out of fitness last term as his career continues to be plagued by such issues.

The severity of the blow is unclear at this stage and his exit from the pitch may have been merely precautionary – but that does not matter given central defence is a problem area that Iraola noted unprompted in his press conference in Chicago earlier this week.

Joe Gomez was forced off injured just nine minutes into Liverpool's win over Sunderland

Jeremy Jacquet, the new boy signed from Rennes who is hoping to play a significant role this term, is not fit and sat out of this friendly. It is understood Liverpool are going carefully with the young Frenchman after he missed half of last season at Rennes, so want to ease him in slowly.

Jacquet’s last game was February 7 and, even if he was to be as good as everyone at the club hopes and expects him to be, he is still only 21 and needs to settle into the physical demands of English football.

Virgil van Dijk is not on this pre-season tour and has been given an extended break, given he played more minutes than any player in Europe last term. The Dutchman is now 35 and is heading into the final year of his contract.

The only other senior centre back is Giovanni Leoni, the teenage Italian who signed from Parma this time last year but only made one appearance in which he ruptured his anterior cruciate ligament and missed the remainder of the season. His recovery is going well but he is still out.

When he is back, his fitness will need to be managed carefully.

It is also worth recalling that Ibrahima Konate, who played 36 of 38 Premier League games last year, left for Real Madrid on a free transfer.

All of these ingredients add up to one conclusion: Liverpool simply must sign a new defender this summer. Failure to do so leaves them incredibly light in that area and it could cost them dearly.

Morrison takes his chance

Defence is not the only area of the pitch where Iraola’s men are light going into the new campaign, which means there will be chances for youngsters to step up.

It has been one of the key themes of pre-season given plenty of senior stars are absent from this trip, including Van Dijk, Alisson, Cody Gakpo, Alexis Mac Allister and new signing Victor Munoz, who won the World Cup with Spain. Which kids can step up?

Here in Nashville, it was Morrison who did just that. A goal in the first half was the highlight after Harvey Elliott – back after a forgettable year at Aston Villa – threaded a nice pass to Morrison, who cut in off the right flank and curled a shot into the bottom corner with his left foot.

Kieran Morrison scored Liverpool's opener in a 4-2 win against Sunderland

The 19-year-old, who can play across the forward line, had several other moments of quality and could have notched an assist or two if luck was more on his side.

Northern Ireland are trying to tie down the Manchester-born teenager, who has one senior cap for the national team (he needs to play three times to ensure England cannot poach him at a later date) – and this performance showed why.

He joined Liverpool as an Under-14, having spent eight years at Manchester United as a kid. With several gaps in the forward line – not to mention a Mohamed Salah-sized hole on the right – could Morrison step up?

We won’t get carried away based on one pre-season outing but he was the man of the match here in Tennessee and Iraola must have been impressed. Manchester United’s loss, it would appear, is Liverpool’s gain.

Which other kids stood out?

While the lack of defensive depth is a glaring issue and a worry for many, two who might be rubbing their hands are teenage duo Mor Talla Ndiaye and Ifeanyi Ndukwe, who both played the majority of this match.

Ndiaye, 18, was signed from Senegalese side Amitie FC in January having caught the eye at the Under-17 World Cup. He is a physical unit, seems calm in possession and is left-footed, which always helps. He has made the first-team bench several times.

Next to him was Austrian youngster Ndukwe, also 18. Signed from Austria Wien in January, Ndukwe officially joined up with his new team this summer. The 6ft 6in defender is another identified by global talent-spotter Matt Newberry in an intriguing recruitment drive.

21-year-old James McConnell impressed in midfield for Liverpool

Both played well and may be needed this season.

Further up the field, James McConnell was impressive in midfield, Calum Scanlon caught the eye on the left flank with several energetic runs and Josh Abe, who only turned 16 earlier this month, had some nice touches.

Lewis Koumas took his goal with composure after a fine move starring also Dominik Szoboszlai, who was wearing the captain’s armband.

Chiesa shows Iraola what he can do

There are several notable shortcomings to Federico Chiesa’s game that have been well documented by fans. But one thing he has that could be desirable to Iraola is versatility.

He can play on the right wing, left or, as he did here, as a No 9. The Italian scored Liverpool’s third with a well-taken finish from a tight angle then he played a lovely round-the-corner ball in the lead-up to Koumas’s goal.

Chiesa has had a weird career at Liverpool. His first season was a write-off, pretty much, due to injury. The next campaign had some bright moments and big goals but, overall, he never earned the trust of Arne Slot.

Many expected he would leave this summer but is he worth keeping around due to his versatility? It is food for thought for Iraola.

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua fights back tears as he dedicates dramatic victory over Kristian Prenga to two best friends killed in car crash as he recovers from TWO knockdowns to win on return
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua fights back tears as he dedicates dramatic victory over Kristian Prenga to two best friends killed in car crash as he recovers from TWO knockdowns to win on return

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Anthony Joshua knows better than anyone how quickly heavyweight boxing can tear up the script. And for a moment on Saturday night in Jeddah, it looked as though another shock was unfolding as the British heavyweight was dropped twice and wrestled to the canvas in a chaotic opening round.

But Joshua dug deep, weathered the storm and, after finding another gear in the second, produced a devastating combination that flattened Albanian heavyweight Kristian Prenga, leaving the 35-year-old sprawled on his back and bringing a dramatic end to a fight that had threatened to derail his comeback before it had even begun.

Although, when AJ's hand was raised, the victory itself almost felt secondary.

For the first time since returning to the ring, the grief that he had worked so hard to suppress finally appeared.

The former two-time heavyweight world champion appeared, perhaps for the first time in public, to let the emotions he had buried since Latif 'Latz' Ayodele and Sina Ghami's tragic deaths in a car crash in Nigeria last December finally surface.

Joshua admitted before the fight that he had spent months suppressing the pain of losing the two men - Latz, his strength coach, and Sina, his personal trainer - insisting he did not want to make their deaths about himself while their families mourned.

Yet, after completing the hardest comeback of his career, both physically and mentally, the emotion could no longer be contained. Joshua broke down during his post-fight interview when crediting his friends for getting him through the first round before quietly saying: 'I don't want to talk about it anymore.'

Anthony Joshua gave an emotional interview after beating Kristian Prenga in Jeddah

When AJ's hand was raised, the victory itself almost felt secondary

Joshua was overcome with emotion after the fight, going from a euphoric high to an emotional low within minutes

For months after the crash, Joshua lived with constant pain. Simply getting out of bed became a struggle. He spent two months gently pedalling on a stationary bike before learning how to balance on a stability ball as he rebuilt his body from the ground up.

While the mental toll must have been every bit as demanding, if not more.

That said, Joshua and Eddie Hearn never liked calling this his 'comeback fight'. Seven months out of the ring is hardly unusual for a heavyweight. He had never truly been away from boxing.

But in every way that mattered, this was a comeback.

Because making it back into the ring after losing two of the people closest to him was perhaps Joshua’s greatest challenge of all.

There were moments when returning to the ring did not feel important, or even possible. But eventually, boxing became part of the healing process.

And so, under the bright lights of the Jeddah Superdome and with Latz and Sina embodied on the canvas, Joshua walked back into battle carrying far more than the pressure of victory on his shoulders.

Prenga was never supposed to be the final destination. The Albanian was always viewed as the bridge to something much bigger.

From the moment the fight was announced, it was understood that the real prize was Fury later this year.

This was the tune-up. The opportunity for Joshua to shake off the ring rust, rebuild momentum and remind the heavyweight division exactly who he is.

That is not to say there was no danger. There always is in the heavyweight division and Joshua was reminded of that the hard way.

Prenga entered the contest with 20 knockouts from 20 victories and just a single defeat. The power was genuine. In heavyweight boxing, one punch can change everything, and for a moment it looked as though it might.

The Albanian dominated a chaotic opening round, dropping Joshua twice and threatening to rip up the script.

Joshua was knocked down twice in the first round

But Joshua recovered in the second round, knocking Kristian Prenga out

It's anticipated that Joshua will finally fight Tyson Fury after both heavyweights won their fights this weekend

But there are levels in elite boxing. Prenga had never shared a ring with anyone approaching Joshua's pedigree or experience, and once the former two-time world champion returned to his corner and received a stern dressing down from his coaching team, he emerged with renewed purpose.

Still showing signs of the defensive vulnerabilities that have haunted him throughout his career, Joshua nevertheless displayed the resilience that has defined his comeback. He turned the tide in emphatic fashion, unleashing a devastating combination to stop Prenga 2:43 into the second round.

When Joshua's hand was raised, the emotion he had worked so hard to suppress could finally be contained no longer.

He had warned beforehand that he had kept so much inside. He did not want to centre himself in a story that belonged to grieving families. He wanted to honour his friends privately.

Instead, he pledged lifelong financial support to both families and vowed to continue pursuing the dreams they all shared together.

Yet as victory was confirmed in Jeddah, it was impossible not to think of everything he had endured to get there.

This was never just another win.

But there was one person missing: Tyson Fury.

Only 24 hours earlier, Fury had fought Mariusz Wach in Thailand, going seven rounds before the veteran Pole retired on his stool in a non-televised contest.

All week Fury had insisted he would not be travelling to Saudi Arabia for Joshua's fight and, despite widespread expectation that he would make a late appearance, the former world champion stayed away.

His absence did little to dampen the belief that British boxing's biggest fight is edging closer, but it denied fans the image they have waited years to see.

After so many failed negotiations, collapsed deals and false starts, supporters had hoped to see Joshua and Fury stand face-to-face in the ring for the first time with both men coming off victories.

But experience has taught Joshua not to assume anything in heavyweight boxing.

His long-awaited showdown with Deontay Wilder appeared all but set before Wilder suffered a shock defeat by Joseph Parker in December 2023 on the very same night Joshua won, sending months of planning into the bin.

The heavyweight division has a habit of snatching away the fights everyone wants to see.

Joshua wore a jacket featuring a medal bar with 'Sina' and 'Latz' pennants

Joshua honoured his friends, Latz and Sina, who were killed in a car crash in December

That is why there will remain a degree of caution until the AJ vs Fury fight is officially confirmed.

Joshua and Eddie Hearn have already revealed that the contract stipulates any showdown with Fury must take place in the United Kingdom because, in their eyes, the biggest fight in British boxing history belongs on British soil.

As things stand, however, Turki Alalshikh and Netflix are understood to favour Madison Square Garden in New York.

That means the contracts will need to be renegotiated.

The expectation is that discussions between all parties will take place over the coming days as they attempt to iron out the remaining details.

For now, Joshua's focus was not on what comes next, but on what he had already overcome.

The tears in Jeddah were not for Tyson Fury.

They were for Latz and Sina.

Sports.title: Adam Ramsay-Peaty kisses pregnant wife Holly's baby bump as he misses out on gold and finishes in third place in the 100m breaststroke final at the Commonwealth Games
Sports.content:
Adam Ramsay-Peaty kissed pregnant wife Holly's baby bump as he missed out on his 33rd major gold medal as he finished in third place in the 100m breaststroke final at the Commonwealth Games on Saturday.

The 18-year-old from Jersey Filip Nowacki finished ahead of his idol in second, but gold went to Australian Sam Williamson.

Williamson finished in 59.17 seconds, while Nowacki was milliseconds behind at 59.34 and Ramsay-Peaty behind him at 59.65.

Despite her husband missing out on the gold, Holly was ever the proud wife as she packed on the PDA with Adam after the medal ceremony.

The swimmer sweetly kissed his wife's growing baby bump before breaking down in tears over his 'hurtful' loss.

He said: 'I'm never afraid to show emotion. It's important because it helps create stronger people, stronger men, stronger fathers and stronger husbands.

'This cycle especially, I've worked harder than ever. To get a result like that hurts because I know I'm better than that.

Adam Ramsay-Peaty kissed pregnant wife Holly's baby bump as he finished in third place in 100m breaststroke final at Commonwealth Games on Saturday

The couple packed on the PDA after the swimmer missed out on his 33rd major gold medal

Adam was the favourite to win the 100m breaststroke final at the Commonwealth Games but only managed to secure third place

'It's still very raw. I honestly feel like I deserve more. There's a lot of thinking to do, but it's too early to draw any conclusions.

'Maybe it was just an off swim. Maybe it's because I've been away from championship racing for two years. I honestly don't know.

'What's the point of all the 5.30am starts? What's the point of all the metres every single day? What's the point of being exhausted all the time, or missing family events because you have to train?

'It has to mean something. For me, that means striving for excellence, and today wasn't excellence. That's where the emotion comes from.

'The choices I've made over the last few months have been difficult. At the same time, I'm proud that I got here and that I didn't quit after Paris [Olympics]. I know I deserve more, and I know I can work for it.

'It's been two years since I've raced heats, semis and finals, so maybe it's just an adjustment. It's too early to know what I'm capable of at this stage, but I'm a fighter.

'We've got another opportunity at the Europeans in two weeks, and I do enjoy a scrap. I lost that scrap today, but that's sport. Most of the time I've won those battles – this time I didn't.'

However, reports of his strained relationship with his parents have clearly taken their toll on Adam, as he added that he can't continue.

He continued: 'Over the last couple of months I've had to make some hard decisions so I could focus on doing my job.

'I've had to ignore a lot of the rubbish people write online. Enough is enough. This goes beyond sport. It's about being decent people. We all have to do better.

'My wife will always be proud of me. As a father, it doesn't matter whether you come home with a gold medal, as long as you come home. That's what really matters.'

Ahead of the Games, Holly, who announced last month she is expecting a baby girl with Adam, couldn't contain her smile as she took her seat to watch her husband, 31, compete in the final.

Holly, who is the daughter of TV chef Gordon Ramsay, 26, showed off her blossoming baby bump in a simple black T-shirt and matching jumper.

His pregnant Holly Ramsay couldn't contain her smile as she arrived to watch husband Adam compete in the final

Following the race, Adam admitted he was disappointed in his result: 'I've worked harder than ever. To get a result like that hurts because I know I'm better than that. It's still very raw'

Holly looked so proud of her husband after the race

Holly showed off her blossoming baby bump in a simple black T-shirt and matching jumper as she showed her support to Adam

The couple hugged after the tense final

The couple packed on the PDA after the race

Adam sweetly kissed Holly's baby bump

The couple looked more loved-up than ever after tying the knot in December

Adam was seen getting ready for the final

During the heats on Friday, Adam won despite a 10-minute delay caused by a detached lane rope.

He posted the fastest qualifying time and advanced comfortably to the semifinals and then progressed through the semifinals to book his place in the final.

The three-time Olympic champion is taking part in his fourth Commonwealth Games having clinched his first medals as a 19-year-old in Glasgow in 2014.

Adam has described these Games as a 'full circle moment' as he looks to reignite his career.

A silver medal at the Paris Olympics in 2024 helped him refocus after a difficult 2023 in which he withdrew from a series of events in order to focus on mental health concerns.

His win in the 100m in 2014 began eight years of almost total dominance in the event. That streak came to an end in dramatic fashion in Birmingham four years ago when he trailed home in a shock fourth place in the event.

Adam told TNT Sports: 'Job done, really. We've got a busy two weeks coming up, so we're reserving energy where we can.

'Last time I was here, I was very young. We barely had any world records to my name, or known world records to my name, so it's been a very long journey.'

Ramsay-Peaty debuted his new name on his swimming cap at the Commonwealth Games as he hopes his new moniker will bring him luck.

The three-time Olympic swimming champion is using his full name for the first time to compete at a major championship after marrying TV chef Gordon Ramsay's daughter Holly last December.

Sadly his parents did not attend the wedding and are assumed to not be attending the Commonwealth Games amid a falling out. Adam remains estranged from them.

Join the discussion Should family come before sporting fame, even if it risks your career?

The daughter of TV chef Gordon Ramsay, 26, looked excited as she took her seat in the crowd to watch her partner, 31

Styling her dark tresses loose, the star wore a radiant palette of makeup and accessorised with a simple cross necklace

The pregnant influencer was spotted staying hydrated in the crowd ahead of Adam competing in the final after he won his heat on Saturday

Holly cheered on Adam from the crowd

Holly was all smiles as she chatted with friends in the stands

The 18-year-old from Jersey Filip Nowacki finished ahead of his idol in second, but gold went to Australian Sam Williamson

Adam debuted his new name Ramsay-Peaty on his swimming cap at the Commonwealth Games as he hopes his new moniker will bring him luck

Earlier this month, the Daily Mail revealed that Adam's pregnant sister Bethany – the only member of his family to still be in contact with the couple – has now sensationally fallen out with Holly.

Not only are they no longer communicating, but this time it is Adam who is stuck in the middle, trying (and so far failing) to mend fences. Read the full story here.

The roots of the family conflict go back to September 2024, when Adam and Holly snubbed wider members of the Peaty family by not inviting them to their engagement party.

Caroline, who spent years ferrying her son to early-morning training sessions, was also not invited to Holly's glamorous hen do at Soho Farmhouse in the Cotswolds, even though the bride's mother, Tana, and friends including Victoria, were at the extravagant bash.

Adam changing his name to Ramsay-Peaty and registering under the double-barrel surname for the Games in Glasgow is the latest blow for his estranged loved ones – especially as Ramsay is placed first before Peaty.

A source said previously: 'Adam may be rich but we have something that he hasn't and that is brains, loyalty, integrity and family.

'Money makes for a cold bedfellow. It can't hold you tight when things go wrong or when you have a bad day.'

They added: 'When you live to be famous you aren't living, you are playing a role. Fame is but fleeting but family is forever.'

Adam's heat was temporarily halted as he was on the blocks when a lane divider broke off, requiring an official to strip to the waist and enter the pool to reconnect it.

The athlete duly wasted no time in recording the fastest time of the morning, 59.46 seconds, with only two rivals, Australia's Sam Williamson and Filip Nowacki of Jersey, also finishing in under a minute.

Adam has described these Games as a 'full circle moment' as he looks to reignite his career.

The influencer announced last month she is expecting a baby girl with Adam

LeBron James has received a major boost in his quest to bring a championship to Philadelphia, with two-time NBA champion Kentavious Caldwell-Pope preparing to join him with the 76ers.

Caldwell-Pope agreed to a contract buyout with the Memphis Grizzlies and plans to sign a one-year, $3.9 million deal with the 76ers after clearing waivers, according to ESPN's Shams Charania.

The move reunites James with his former Los Angeles Lakers teammate, with whom he previously won the 2020 NBA championship inside the Orlando bubble.

The veteran star brings elite capabilities to a transformed Philadelphia roster, providing elite perimeter defense alongside proven championship experience.

Caldwell-Pope earned his second championship ring in 2023 as a starter for the Nuggets, proving his status as one of the league's most reliable shooting guards.

His arrival bolsters a loaded 76ers squad that has undergone a dramatic offseason overhaul to build an immediate title contender around Joel Embiid and Tyrese Maxey.

LeBron James has received a major boost in his quest to bring a championship to Philadelphia

Two-time NBA champion Kentavious Caldwell-Pope is preparing to join James with the 76ers

The acquisition comes just days after James stunned the basketball world by taking a historic pay cut, signing a two-year, $8 million veteran deal to join Philadelphia.

By accepting a salary below market value, James allowed the 76ers' front office flexibility to construct a championship-caliber supporting cast around their new core.

Caldwell-Pope's addition addresses a critical need on the wing, providing head coach Nick Nurse with an experienced lockdown defender capable of spacing the floor for Embiid and James.

With James, Embiid, Maxey, Jaylen Brown and now Caldwell-Pope in the fold, Philadelphia has firmly positioned itself as a favorite in the Eastern Conference.

As training camp approaches, the 76ers' aggressive summer spending spree signals a clear, all-in mandate to deliver the franchise's first NBA title since 1983.

Shortly after James' move to Philadelphia was confirmed, President Donald Trump launched an astonishing attack on the NBA legend.

On Friday, Trump was asked to weigh in on who holds the title of the greatest basketball player of all time.

'Michael Jordan's a guy that's a friend of mine, I've played golf with him,' Trump said.

The news comes days after James stunned the basketball world by taking a historic pay cut

The move reunites James with his former Los Angeles Lakers teammate, with whom he previously won the 2020 NBA championship

'He's a really good guy and I think LeBron is - maybe he's a racist, but maybe he doesn't like Trump, I don't know - but I only like people that like me, so I would say Michael Jordan all the way.'

The comments mark the latest chapter in a long-standing feud between the four-time NBA champion and Trump, which dates back to James labeling him a 'bum' in 2017.

James, 41, has frequently used his platform to criticize Trump, previously endorsing Democratic candidates and launching voting-rights initiatives across the country.

Their bad blood spilled into the public eye during Trump's first presidency after he withdrew a White House invitation extended to Golden State Warriors star Steph Curry over his hesitation to visit.

Sports.title: 'Hurt' Adam Ramsay-Peaty breaks down in tears after surprise Commonwealth Games bronze: Star reveals family feud has taken its toll and admits he 'doesn't know what went wrong'
Sports.content:
First came an apology. 'Sorry guys,' said Adam Ramsay-Peaty, as his voice began to tremble. He wiped away a tear from his face and stared at the Tollcross floor to find his words.

The bronze medal around his neck felt like a heavy weight. 'It's hard because I know how hard I've worked. I know the s**t I've been through, which is no fault of my own. It does take a toll.'

After standing upon the podium, the 31-year-old walked around the pool and stopped for selfies with his adoring fans. An Englishman has not received a reception like this in Glasgow for a long time.

He stopped to hug his pregnant wife, Holly – the daughter of celebrity chef Gordon Ramsay – before kissing her pregnant stomach. They are expecting a daughter in December and, as the swimmer confessed, family life has changed his priorities.

'She's always super proud of me,' he said. 'As a father, it doesn't matter if you come home with the gold, as long as you come home with the teddy, which I did. That's what matters.

'As you can tell, the emotion is always something that I'm going to carry. I'm never going to be afraid to show weakness because it's so important for making stronger people, making stronger men, stronger fathers, stronger husbands.

'I think 'S**t, how have I worked so hard at this age?' - then you get a result like that. I'm better than that. Maybe it's because I've had two years out, but it does hurt. There's a lot going on in my head right now.'

Adam Ramsay-Peaty was brought to tears as he reflected 'I'm never going to be afraid to show weakness' after securing bronze at the Commonwealth games

Adam Ramsay-Peaty stopped to hug his pregnant wife, Holly - the daughter of celebrity chef Gordon Ramsay - before kissing her pregnant stomach

The pair wed on December 27 last year at Bath Abbey

Ramsay-Peaty was chasing from the start. He was not the leader of the pack. Perhaps he will fare better over 50 metres but here, over two lengths, he finished almost three seconds off his world record.

Australian Sam Williamson won gold and 18-year-old Filip Nowacki, of Jersey, claimed a brilliant silver that bodes well for the future of British swimming.

'I'm not crying because it's a bronze instead of a gold,' said Peaty, choking up throughout. 'I'm crying because I know that swim could have been better. I don't really know what went wrong in these last two weeks but something isn't hitting right, whether it's pace or focus.

'I feel like I couldn't have put more in, so you ask, 'What's the point of all the 5.30ams. What's the point of all the metres every day? What's the point of feeling exhausted all the time? What's the point of saying, 'No' to all the family events because of training?' It's because you want excellence and that isn't excellence for me.

'I enjoy a scrap but I lost that scrap in the last 25 metres. That's sport. Most of the time I've won the scrap. For some reason, the Commonwealths is that humble reminder.'

The wedding stories, the family feud and the social media abuse have taken their toll. The pool should be his place of escape but he swam with the world on his shoulders.

'People who comment and read headlines have got to look themselves in the mirror. Ignoring that comes at a cost. That hasn't played a part in that result here but it has to stop. Do better. I don't want young Filip to go through that.'

Ramsay-Peaty was overcome with emotion in the mixed zone reflecting on his bronze medal

Throughout his decorated career, Ramsay-Peaty has been so far ahead of the field that he has had to look in the mirror to find competition. He has broken 14 world records, asserting a similar dominance to Sweden's serial pole vault champion Armand Duplantis. Untouchables. Now people will ask if time is finally catching up with Britain's greatest swimmer.

Nowacki is still waiting for his A Level results but the schoolboy from Millfield has already beaten his idol's teenage records. In 2012, Jason Kenny beat Chris Hoy to become the top dog of cycling. Lamine Yamal overcame Lionel Messi in last week's World Cup final. Swimming insiders believe it is a matter of time until Nowacki pulls a similar stunt.

'For me, he's got a very bright future ahead of him,' said Ramsay-Peaty, whose gold earrings caught the light of the cameras. 'He's my favourite for the 200m. He's definitely got the speed and he's about 25kgs less! He's got many many miles ahead of him, whereas my miles are probably coming to an end. I guess two years isn't that long to try and find that in me.'

Side by side, they look like David and Goliath. Nowacki is five inches shorter and does not have the same popping biceps. Ramsay-Peaty changed the game with his powerful upper body stroke but Nowacki's strength is in his kick. He keeps his hips high and moves more gracefully than his senior, who forces his way through the water.

Nowacki will discover his maths, economics and physics exam results during next month's European Championships. Then he plans to enrol at Loughborough University, where he can master his craft in time for the LA 2028 Olympics. Major medals are in his sights, although Ramsay-Peaty is not ready to stand aside just yet.

'To be racing one of the best in the world – arguably the greatest breaststroker of all time – is very special to me,' said Nowacki, who won the world junior championships last year in a time of 2:07.32, which would have medalled in every senior Olympics, bar one

Ramsay-Peaty knows a promising swimmer when he sees one. He has already signed up Nowacki to his own agency and will continue to mentor his prodigy.

'If I compare myself to 2014, 12 years ago, it's very exciting where Filip and his career can go,' he said. 'It's sport, it's beautiful, but f**k me, it can hurt.'

Sports.title: Sole British contender Kalpana stuns favourite to surge to impressive victory in King George VI And Queen Elizabeth Stakes at Ascot
Sports.content:
Sole British contender Kalpana stuns favourite to surge to impressive victory in King George VI And Queen Elizabeth Stakes at Ascot

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Sole British contender Kalpana saw off a stellar international field to hand trainer Andrew Balding an emotional first victory in the King George VI And Queen Elizabeth Stakes.

Ascot's Group One showpiece has been synonymous with the Balding family since Andrew's late father, Ian, won it with his legendary Derby winner Mill Reef in 1971.

'It is a big deal as it is a race we have always wanted to win,' said a visibly emotional Balding, who sent out a rapid Group race treble in the space of two hours — thanks to Moonrise's success in the Princess Margaret Stakes earlier on the card and Item's Group Two win at York.

'It defines a season, and it defines a career a race like this. I'm so pleased.'

Referring to his family's legacy with the race, Balding added: 'We have grown up with it. I think the first ever winner of the race was trained at Kingsclere [where Balding trains], it is lovely to bring it back all these years later.'

For his part, jockey Colin Keane was a little more measured, saying: 'I'm just delighted for the filly. Although she's won two Group Ones, she probably deserves to have won a couple more and she showed her true class today.

'It was one of the strongest renewals of the race, with horses coming from all over the globe, so for her to go and do it today is very special.'

Kalpana saw off a stellar international field to hand trainer Andrew Balding an emotional first victory

In a race run at a furious gallop, courtesy of two Ballydoyle pacemakers, Mickael Barzalona adopted patient tactics aboard reigning champion Calandagan before attempting to reel in Kalpana from the two-furlong marker.

However, in contrast to 12 months ago, the 6-5 favourite could not overhaul Balding's mare who kept on powerfully to score by a cosy length and a half, with Irish Derby winner Benvenuto Cellini a creditable third.

While disappointed at his gelding's defeat, Calandagan's trainer, Francis-Henri Graffard, was content with the performance.

'This season hasn't been as smooth as last year,' Graffard said.

'Epsom [Calandagan finished fourth in the Coronation Cup] was a disaster and then, Saint-Cloud, he won a good race there but they had changed the date of the race and it was much closer to this race.

'So, it gave me less time to get him very fresh for today and, also, it's a heatwave in France — it takes a lot of energy of the horses. So with all these factors he still ran a very good race.'

Master trainer Aidan O'Brien was also content with the efforts of Benvenuto Cellini, who saw out the 1m 4f trip well.

He said: 'I was very happy with Benvenuto Cellini. He ran a great race. It was his first time against the older horses, and we learnt a lot about him.

'We learnt he gets the mile and a half well, and you couldn't be sure of that until he did it against the older horses. Even going to the line he didn't looked finished.

'I think we could look at the Breeders' Cup.'

Unfortunately, there were few positives in the performances of Japanese contenders Masquerade Ball and Wurttemberg, who never figured in seventh and ninth respectively.

Away from the big race here on a sunny Berkshire afternoon, Saffie Osborne rode a sparkling 274-1 treble, with superb victories aboard Amazing Journey and Hickory, for her father Jamie, and Primo Lara for trainer Jane Chapple-Hyam.

'I love Ascot and it has been very lucky for me, with the exception of the Royal meeting,' enthused the thrilled rider. 'All three horses

had a chance but it would have been a bit adventurous to think they would all win. It's very special.'

Chapple-Hyam enjoyed two winners herself at the track yesterday, with the Ryan Moore-ridden Kon Tiki impressively capturing the Group Three Valiant Stakes to supplement Primo Lara's later victory.

Hamzah Sheeraz was a lacklustre winner in the second world title fight of the night, ultimately winning a majority decision over Simon Zachenhuber. Sheeraz only won his super-middleweight strap nine weeks ago in front of the Pyramids of Giza and looked laboured throughout his first defence.

Sports.title: British Paralympics medallist insists 'I never cheated' after receiving brutal two-year ban
Sports.content:
British Paralympics medallist insists 'I never cheated' after receiving brutal two-year ban

Paralympic cyclist Daphne Schrager was banned for two years after failing a drugs test

View 2 Images Daphne Schrager (Image: Adam Davy/PA Wire)

British Paralympic medalist Daphne Schrager has stated that she has “never cheated” after she was handed a two-year ban for failing a drugs test. Schrager, a para-cyclist, won a silver medal for Great Britain during the 2024 Paralympics in Paris.

‌



An out-of-competition drug test in April 2025 found that Schrager had tested positive for Ligandrol, a substance on the banned list that can increase muscle and bone mass.

‌



Schrager, who is from Malmesbury, has made it clear that she has never used banned substances and argued that exposure through environmental contamination was the reason for the positive test.

‌



Two potential scenarios were presented, including a massage she had received at a gym, or at a shared residential address.

However, a National Anti-Doping Panel tribunal determined that while Schrager had not deliberately used a banned substance, she had not demonstrated that it was an accidental environmental contamination.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! All the best sports news and much more on our dedicated Facebook page

‌



Consequently, the 25-year-old was issued a two-year ban from competition, which has been backdated to commence from the date of her initial suspension on June 2, 2025, and will conclude on June 1, 2027.

The two-year rather than the four-year ban does leave the possibility open for Schrager to potentially participate at the 2028 Paralympic Games in Los Angeles. In a lengthy statement posted on Instagram, Schrager revealed she had commissioned hair and nail analysis in an attempt to prove her innocence - yet as the precise origin of the contamination could not be pinpointed, the ban was upheld.

"In June last year, I received news that turned my world upside down," she said. "I had tested positive in an anti-doping test for a trace amount of Ligandrol, detected at 0.0006ng, resulting in my suspension from cycling since that time.

‌



"I want to be very clear: I have never cheated, nor have I ever knowingly taken any banned substance. Facing the possibility of a four-year ban unless I could prove that the result was unintentional has been incredibly distressing."

The tribunal was told that Schrager firmly denied ever using prohibited substances and maintained that she had never deliberately breached the ADR.

She provided testimony that the presence of Ligandrol was the result of environmental contamination rather than deliberate use, either through exposure at the gym she visited two days prior to her sample being collected, or alternatively, through environmental contamination within her shared home.

‌



View 2 Images Daphne Schrager (Image: Adam Davy/PA Wire)

The Tribunal considered scientific evidence from a number of experts, alongside additional testimony. The experts were in agreement that inadvertent environmental contamination was responsible for the positive test, concluding that Schrager had not intentionally used Ligandrol.

The Tribunal was also convinced, on the balance of probabilities, that there was no recklessness in Schrager's attendance at the gym, but they observed that as Schrager had not established how Ligandrol entered her system, she had unintentionally committed anti-doping offences and thus imposed her two-year period of ineligibility.

‌



"In cases like mine, by the time an athlete is informed of their positive test, too much time has passed to identify the exact source of contamination with the certainty that the rules demand," Schrager added. "That is not a failure of honesty or effort, it is simply too much of a burden to be met in every case.

"This is one of the most difficult periods of my life. Losing my contract, my team and the structure that had long shaped my purpose and identity left me facing a level of uncertainty I had never known."

Schrager, who has cerebral palsy, described the impact on her mental health as "significant and at times overwhelming" - yet vowed to make her comeback in 2027.

Article continues below

She secured ParalympicsGB's first medal of the 2024 Games, claiming silver in the women's C1-3 3,000m individual pursuit.

She later won two gold medals at the Para-cycling Road World Cup in May 2025 in the C2 class – before being suspended just a month later.

Sports.title: Sean McCann misses out on medal but Commonwealth Games dream isn't over
Sports.content:
Sean McCann misses out on medal but Commonwealth Games dream isn't over

Sean McCann - the younger brother of Madeleine McCann - competed in the men's 400m freestyle swimming final at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow and was supported by his family in the crowd

View 3 Images Scotland's Sean McCann reacts after the Men's 400m Freestyle Final (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Sean McCann missed out on a medal as he finished last in the men's 400m freestyle swimming final at the Commonwealth Games. McCann, 21, finished 12 seconds off the pace for Scotland in a race which saw Australia take gold, silver and bronze.

‌



Sam Short topped the podium, with Elijah Winnington and Benjamin Goedemans finishing second and third respectively. England's James Guy narrowly missed out on the bronze model after being bumped down to fourth late in the race. Northern Ireland's Daniel Wiffen came fifth.

‌



Backed by a home crowd, McCann got a huge cheer when he emerged for the final in Glasgow.

‌



View 3 Images Kate & Gerry McCann cheering on Sean (Image: Stuart Wallace/Shutterstock)

He was two years old when older sister Madeleine went missing during a family holiday in Portugal in May 2007. Her disappearance remains one of the world's most high-profile missing person cases, with Metropolitan Police still investigating nearly two decades later.

‌

Sean's dad, Gerry, and mum Kate were in the crowd alongside twin sister Amelie at the Tollcross Swimming Centre. Their son had come fourth in his heat and crept through to the final.

Article continues below

McCann is a student at Loughborough University, where he trains and studies chemical engineering. Having grown up in England, he qualifies for Scotland through his dad.

The 21-year-old still has a chance to win a first Commonwealth Games medal, as he'll compete in the 800m and 1500m freestyle events later in the meet. McCann's dream is to represent Team GB at the Olympic Games.

Speaking after his heat, he said: "The Olympics is always that step even further. Being able to represent Scotland is a good stepping stone on the way to that. Hopefully a couple more years work I will be in the mix for the Olympics."

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."

Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat

World Cup play-off finals - Europe Bosnia & Herzegovina vs Italy

Sweden vs Poland

Kosovo vs Turkey

Czech Republic vs Denmark

How Ireland threw away their lead

Ireland came flying out the blocks flying in Prague. Four shots in the opening ten minutes, including Nathan Collins crashing a shot off the bar from range, set the tone for a brilliant display - and they got their rewards.

A long throw caused chaos and Nathan Collins was deemed to have been caught slightly late by Vladimir Darida by VAR, who sent referee Glenn Byberg to the monitor for a review.

Troy Parrott, who else, crashed in the penalty for his sixth goal in the last three Ireland matches. And it got better for Ireland four minutes later.

Ryan Manning's corner found Dara O'Shea at the back post and his header across was cleared off the line by Vladimir Coufal - but off goalkeeper Matej Kovar and over the line.

Image: Czech Republic goalkeeper Matej Kovar scores an own goal to give Ireland a 2-0 lead

Ireland were in dreamland but a moment of Manning madness brought the Czech Republic back into it. The defender's needless tug back on Krekci - when the ball was heading out of play - was penalised by referee Byberg, with Patrick Schick pulling one back from the spot.

Ireland did, however, manage to settle the nerves down - right throughout the second half. Despite sustained Czech pressure in the second half, they barely threatened.

It was Ireland who had the better chances after the break, with Jayson Molumby striking the post and Parrott denied by a solid Kovar save at a corner. But then heartbreak struck with four minutes of normal time remaining, as Krejci bundled the ball in at the near post from a set piece.

Krejci could have even won it with the last kick of the game but scuffed his finish, as extra-time came.

Substitute Tomas Soucek missed a glorious chance for the hosts, with Adam Idah was denied a one-on-one chance by a goal-saving challenge from Stepan Chaloupek. Penalties came and the lottery fell in the hosts' favour.

Image: Jan Kliment scored the winning goal in the penalty shoot-out

Hallgrimsson confident in Ireland future despite 'pain'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"One word is pain. I feel pain. I feel pride for the performance of the players. They gave it all. I feel gratitude for all the supporters who supported us through the whole game, even after the loss. I feel pride being a part of that group. Personally, I know all the players will feel pain now. Only pain.

"We take with us that we can play teams higher in the FIFA ranking and can punch above our weight: Portugal, Hungary and here. We can compete with these teams. We came here with three wins in a row, a long time since that happened for this national team.

"So there's growth in this squad. It's maturing. These are been the biggest game most of these players have played. That's encouraging to know we're growing. It's strange to say that after we lost today.

"I know I'm biased in this, all the statistics and metrics of the team have improved. Big games, being on the line, crunch times all the time, we've managed to go through this. It showed the resilience, character of these players, that's why I feel confident going on."

Sports.title: Wilson key for Wales, NI aim for big upset while history beckons for ROI
Sports.content:
Sky Sports assesses Thursday's 2026 World Cup play-off semi-finals as Wales host Bosnia-Herzegovina, Northern Ireland go to four-time winners Italy and the Republic of Ireland face Czech Republic in Prague.

Thursday 7.45pm: Wales vs Bosnia-Herzegovina (winner will play Italy or Northern Ireland)

Harry Wilson is not the new Gareth Bale, but he's doing the job of Bale at his best, especially for Wales.

Fans have long been excited about Wilson's natural talent, but are now seeing his influence in the Premier League on a weekly basis for Fulham. This season, he has 10 goals and six assists for club, while for country, his stats are even better with five goals and two assists in his last five games.

If Wilson starts running the show, his confidence will feed to the other players and to the home crowd, and Wales will be very difficult to stop on their own patch.

Which World Cup group would Wales be in? If Wales qualify for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Craig Bellamy wanted to create an identity for Wales when he took over as head coach. It's now clear: he wants front-foot football coupled with intensity and energy.

Bellamy doesn't always see that in international football as he finds it slower at times compared with club football, but his Wales side will not be ponderous. You could see during the qualification campaign that Wales' intensity in winning the ball back very quickly and holding possession grew. Now it's about consistently doing it.

Apart from consistency in play, there needs to be consistency in selection. Much is always made about the 'spine' of a good team, from the goalkeeper to the glory hunter! Leeds United provide a fair chunk of Wales' spine with 'keeper Karl Darlow on form and in receipt of the No.1 keeper's jersey. Joe Rodon is the rock at centre-back that success relies upon, while team-mate Ethan Ampadu's versatility means he can link anywhere between defence and midfield. Throw in one of the in-form Premier League stars, Harry Wilson, and a strong spine can take a team a long way.

Ask Bellamy if he has thought about preparing for the play-off final against either Italy or Northern Ireland and you'll get glared at. It's Bosnia, Bosnia and Bosnia. He won't entertain anything beyond Bosnia until the game is over. It's a danger, a banana skin he wants to avoid. Thinking too far ahead isn't good on this occasion.

Geraint Hughes

Thursday 7.45pm: Italy vs Northern Ireland (winner will play Wales or Bosnia-Herzegovina)

On paper, perhaps in reality, it's David vs Goliath.

Northern Ireland enjoy David vs Goliath. Once upon a time it was David (Healy) vs England and David (Healy) vs Spain.

For smaller nations there is comfort in being the underdog. A loss would be met without a major backlash, a win makes you a hero. That's how Michael O'Neill's side will approach Thursday's assignment in Bergamo against Italy.

Which World Cup group would Northern Ireland be in? If Northern Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Conor Bradley and Daniel Ballard are out. Between them they represent 50 per cent of the Northern Ireland players currently plying their trade in the Premier League.

The pair's absence is as much a blow to Northern Ireland's attacking prospects as it is defensively. Ballard represents their best aerial threat from set-pieces, Bradley their most dynamic player on the ball.

And yet for some reason that only football can explain, hope remains. The four-time World Cup winners are heavy favourites but far from the Azzurri powerhouse of old.

If Northern Ireland have it their way, it's unlikely to be a pretty spectacle. But can they frustrate their hosts? 0-0 at half-time? Pounce on the sense of angst that will exist among the home support?

To call it a free hit would be to downplay the importance of the game. But Northern Ireland are free from the weight of expectation.

Daring to dream of a result that becomes instant folklore.

Michael Morrow

Thursday 7.45pm: Czech Republic vs Republic of Ireland (winner will play Denmark or North Macedonia)

Image: Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson and captain Seamus Coleman spoke to the media in Prague

History beckons for the Republic of Ireland here in Prague.

Make no mistake, this will be the biggest game to date for a lot of these Irish players as they attempt to take another step to this summer's World Cup but they must get past Czech Republic to do so.

Which World Cup group would Republic of Ireland be in? If the Republic of Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group A with co-hosts Mexico, South Africa and South Korea.

Still coming off the euphoria of the incredible back-to-back wins against Portugal and Hungary last November, this is an Irish team full of confidence.

Having spoken to a few people around the Czech Republic team, those results have been noted and they are particularly worried about Irish striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in those two games in November - including the 96th-minute winner against Hungary.

Head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson spoke ahead of this game about one of the key aspects is visually and mentally being ready for the challenge ahead of them, he seemed as calm and confident as usual.

However his key selection dilemma is does he bring back the experienced, tried and tested players such as Seamus Coleman, Robbie Brady and Chiedoze Ogbene - all three have had limited game-time this season for a variety of injuries.

Coleman and Brady especially are the only two players in the squad who were part of Ireland's last team in a major tournament which was in 2016 - their experience could prove vital.

Image: Can Troy Parrott recreate his Irish heroics in Prague on Thursday?

Their opponents are in a state of flux.

Czech Republic have a new head coach who takes charge of his first game on Thursday, with West Ham's Tomas Soucek also being stripped of the captaincy after November's internationals having caused shockwaves in the local media - Wolves' Ladislav Krejci has replaced him.

The pressure feels like it's all on the home side which could play into Ireland's advantage as they look to take another step to qualify for this summer's World Cup - their first since 2002.

Danyal Khan
