World.title: Century-old diary sheds new light on life in the Goldfields
World.content:
Historians from opposite sides of the globe have solved a century-old mystery, identifying the author of a diary penned during one of Australia's biggest gold rushes.

Gordon Howard Tilly arrived in Kalgoorlie-Boulder, 600km east of Perth, in 1911, as thousands flocked to make their fortune on the region's 'Golden Mile'.

"If you see a girl dressed in a plush dress with kid gloves and a dainty hat carrying a fancy bag you may be sure that her father pushes a truck under the presses," wrote Gordon Tilly in 1911. (ABC Goldfields: Nicholas R Ward)

His diary, donated to the Leintwardine Historical Society, in Herefordshire, England in 2025, has become a source of fascination for local historians.

Mr Tilly kept obsessive notes that tracked everything from breakfast to stationery prices, providing a window to the past, helping historians better understand the turn of the century on the Eastern Goldfields.

But Mr Tilly omitted one key detail — his name.

From opposite sides of the world

Vivian Simkins, archivist of the Leintwardine Historical Society, said the diary immediately caught her attention.

Mr Tilly's diary was found in the small town of Leintwardine, 200km north-west of London. (ABC Goldfields: Nicholas R Ward)

"We thought, what's this diary about Australia doing in a place like Leintwardine? How did it get here?" she said.

"A friend in the village who was born here, grew up here … when her parents died, she was left with lots of papers and information.

"She brought me this journal, and had no idea where it had come from or who it was by, because … there's no signature in the book.

" Without a name, it was impossible to work out who he was. "

Ms Simkins tried searching the passenger lists for the steam ship Malwa which carried Mr Tilly to Australia but the lists were incomplete and the author of the diary remained elusive.

Hitting a wall in the UK, she contacted the Eastern Goldfields Historical Society (EGHS) in Kalgoorlie-Boulder for help.

"That's when I thought, oh, I'll try the Goldfields and see if they know anything about it," she said.

"And they had the same problem. Who is this man?"

In 1911, Mr Tilly worked as an electrical engineer. A century later, his diary has found a home at the old Boulder power station. (Supplied: Eastern Goldfields Historical Society)

What followed was a six month effort culminating in the diary retracing the author's footsteps back to the Goldfields.

After talking with people at the EGHS, the Leintwardine Society decided the diary should return to where it was written.

"I was due to go out to Australia anyway, I thought I'll take it out," Ms Simkins said.

And in April 2026 over a century after it's departure Mr Tilly's diary arrived back in the Goldfields and into the hands of Rosie Stroud.

There and back again

"His nickname was Tilly, from that information, we couldn't really identify him," EGHS Executive Officer Ms Stroud said.

One volunteer painstakingly transcribed the diary while others combed over records to uncover Mr Tilly's name. (ABC Goldfields: Nicholas R Ward)

With the diary in hand, volunteers at the EGHS painstakingly transcribed the handwritten work and tracked down the complete passenger lists of the Malwa, finally cracking the mystery.

"We love a good story like this," Ms Stroud said.

" People, we can really delve into the history, what was happening at that specific time on the Golden Mile, how people lived, how much money he spent. "

"Boulder city is the less fashionable of the two places but is nearer work," wrote Gordon Tilly. (Supplied: Eastern Goldfields Historical Society)

What emerged was an image far from the stereotype of a turn-of-the-century miner.

"He was a teetotaller, so he didn't drink beer, but he would have a cup of tea and enjoy some quiet time around the area," Ms Stroud said.

A singular man

Gordon Howard Tilly was 22 when he left England aboard the Malwa for a new life as an electrical engineer, arriving in Kalgoorlie-Boulder on May 18, 1911.

While working at the Ivanhoe gold mine (pictured), Mr Tilly recorded narrowly avoiding death when rock loaded with TNT was accidentally sent to the crusher. (Supplied: JJ Dwyer/Eastern Goldfields Historical Society)

"The people are as a rule quiet and nice in public places, broad minded and sensible, willing to do one a good turn and, in common with all people except the English, always ready to start a conversation," Mr Tilly wrote.

" I cannot refrain from the one little grumble I have though, they will use the accursed 'A', there is no need to explain this further. "

Mr Tilly lived near his work at the Ivanhoe mine where he initially worked in the crushing room. (Supplied: Eastern Goldfields Historical Society)

Aside from his work, Mr Tilly enjoyed a number of hobbies.

"The staple pleasure are pictures, skating, and billiards. I did not patronise the last," he wrote.

"The prices for pictures are … one shilling six pence [£0.18] … [Skating is] one shilling six pence the two (I don't know much about it having been only twice).

Skating was a popular pastime a century ago and the Kalgoorlie "hippodrome" once welcomed generations of skaters to the city. (ABC Goldfields: Nicholas R Ward)

"When a theatrical company comes up there is huge excitement."

During his time Mr Tilly took copious notes on shopping, weather, people, and every other detail that caught his eye down to his breakfast.

"Put bacon in the pan and laid the table, I then cut bread… made the tea and Sid's tea etc," he wrote.

"Breakfast is always started at 6 sharp."

But despite seeming to enjoy his new life, he missed his family and wished his mother could visit him.

Hockey Polo, a style of field hockey played on rollerskates, was popular in 1911. (ABC Goldfields: Nicholas R Ward)

For future generations

Mr Tilly was did not stay in Kalgoorlie-Boulder long, moving to Adelaide in 1913 then returning to the UK in 1916 to fight in World War I.

A transcript of Mr Tilly's diary has been made by the Goldfields Historical Society. (ABC Goldfields: Nicholas R Ward)

What happened to him over the rest of his life remains to be uncovered.

The Leintwardine Historical Society continues to dig into his life, and has recently tracked down his great niece.

Despite his short time in the outback, his diary forms an integral part of understanding the gold rush era.

"We can use it then to go on to exhibitions, connect with family, enrich educational programs," Ms Stroud said.

"So this kind of information is pretty good to have."

Mr Tilly's diary will now be preserved in the archives of the Eastern Goldfields Historical Society. (ABC Goldfields: Nicholas R Ward)

Mr Tilly's diary is now safely stored in archival paper at the EGHS to preserve it for the future.

A transcript of the diary is available for the public at the historical society's offices at the old Boulder power station.

World.title: Love story: How Tom and Huma Busby became the perfect duo
World.content:
When singer Tom Busby and his musical partner Jeremy Marou were wrapping up their first major national tour as Busby Marou in Sydney in 2011, the last thing he expected was to meet the love of his life.

Fifteen years later, Tom and his now-wife Huma are embarking on their own tour of Australia, and they're taking their four children along for the ride.

Whether it's romantic, platonic, heartbreaking or surprising, our Love Story series is about love in all its forms. Share yours with us.

Huma: I'm from Houston, Texas, originally. I'd been [in Australia] for about four years, and an Australian friend of mine named Josh wanted to see if we could catch up and go see a band that he managed, which was Tom's band. We met that night and Tom was wearing a blue velvet jacket.

Tom: It was fake [velvet], but I was looking good. It was 2011 and it was the last show of the first big Busby Marou tour. It was a really good, fun time … but I wasn't looking to meet my [future] wife. Me and Huma hung out all weekend and nothing really happened; I still wasn't sure whether she liked me.

Tom and Huma had a long-distance relationship for about a year and a half after they met in Sydney. (Supplied: Huma Busby)

We started talking on Facebook and keeping in contact. Three or four months later, I came back to Sydney and I pulled out the big guns. We were supporting Pete Murray, so I was like, "come backstage," but Huma didn't even know who he was. We started technically seeing each other after that and it was long distance; we dated for about a year and a half.

Rocky road to marriage

Tom: I brought Huma up to Rockhampton. I'm the youngest of eight, so I have all these nieces and nephews and there were about 30 of them there. It was chaos for her, but she was so excited.

It's a big deal to bring anyone back to meet the family. You never bring a girlfriend back unless it's going to be serious.

Huma: Growing up, it was just me and my sister and my mum, so a tiny [family] … but [the Busbys] were the most beautiful, welcoming family and they just took me in.

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

I felt like I was home from the moment I set foot in that door, but I fell in love with him no matter what straight away. We got engaged after about a year and a half together and married in 2014.

When two becomes six

Huma: When we met, Tom said he wanted eight kids and I was like, "huh?" Then I went to my first Busby Christmas, and I was like, "Oh my God, I could have a million of these kids." Then we had our first kid, Freddy (Winifred), who's beautiful. We were like, "that was tough; maybe we should [only] have one," but we met in the middle and had four.

(Clockwise from far left) Winifred, Marigold, Henrietta and Herbie Busby. (Supplied: Huma Busby)

We've got three girls — Winifred, Marigold and Henrietta — and a boy, Herbert. The eldest is 10 and the youngest is four.

Tom: I was on tour a lot but luckily, I never missed a birth. They're all extremely special and I got to be around a lot, but I was also always leaving to go on tour. It's easier when they're younger, but the older they get … it's hard. Their personalities come out. [I] miss them and most importantly, Huma's working and doing it all on her own.

Taking the family on tour

Huma: We went to America for six weeks last year, for a family holiday and to record Tom's album. That was a big leap because we'd never all been together for six weeks it and was the best time of our life.

Busby Marou portray a 'positive message in reconciliation' The musical duo has previously been apolitical, but feel it's time to speak out.

[In Australia], Tom was playing at these awesome bucket-list gigs like Big Red Bash [in Birdsville], Mundi Mundi [near Broken Hill] or Way Out West [in Winton]. The kids and I would be at home, which is fine, but we always thought we need to take them to some of these places.

Tom: Over the last couple of years, it was like we were single parenting. I would go away and Huma was left with all of it, plus her work. Then she'd go away for work and I'm running the business and doing it all on my own as well; we were becoming ships in the night.

Busby Marou were having a break and I had my first solo album [Rockhampton Hangover] coming out. Getting it off the ground again is like going back to the start of Busby Marou, so we thought, let's travel around in the caravan for a while, build my social media profile and come up with a strategy so I can be a long-term career artist. We're literally just living off my gigs, but we're happier and we're working towards something.

Tom and Huma Busby are embarking on a trip around Australia with their four children. (Supplied: Huma Busby)

Huma: Today was our first day of homeschool with the kids; Tom was working and I was doing that. Life's simple and there's less to think about … it sounds cliche, we have less, but we've got a lot more.

I reckon our bond is stronger already, I definitely feel less tension in the marriage, strangely, because it's probably where you're going to feel the most tense, because you're shoved in this caravan that you're towing.

Tom: What I'm hoping and thinking, when we come back home — in a year, two years — is we'll have stopped racing, or if we are racing, it's for the right reasons and not [because] we're juggling 1,000 things.

I really believe that it needs to be a simpler life back in the real world and this has already brought us closer together. We're sharing the job load and the mental load and all of the loads. I feel like this caravan helps with that; there's not much to do, but you have your own little roles.

World.title: Three dead after horror night on Queensland roads
World.content:
A woman and man have died after a collision between a motorbike and pedestrian on the Sunshine Coast.

The 68-year-old woman was walking across Nicklin Way in Warana when she was hit by a motorbike at around 8pm on Saturday.

Police said the woman and the 30-year-old male rider died at the scene.

In a separate crash in Logan around 10:42pm a man was killed and two others seriously injured.

Police said a car travelling south on Kingston Road collided with another car at the Parramatta Road intersection in Underwood.

A male passenger in the second car, aged in his 30s, died at the scene.

The female driver was taken to hospital where she remains in a critical condition while another male passenger is in a stable condition.

The driver of the other car was uninjured.

Police are appealing to the public to come forward with information and any relevant video footage.

World.title: Teen charged over fatal NT crash involving allegedly stolen vehicle
World.content:
A 16-year-old boy has been charged with a string of offences following a fatal crash involving an allegedly stolen vehicle in Katherine last month.

The vehicle rolled on the Stuart Highway about 3 kilometres north of Katherine just before 6am on June 2, killing a 16-year-old boy.

Another five teenagers found at the crash site — two girls aged 16 and 17, two 15-year-old boys, and a 13-year-old boy — were taken to hospital with minor injuries.

At the time, Northern Territory police said another 16-year-old boy was also identified as an occupant of the vehicle after going to a local clinic with minor injuries.

Police were called to the crash scene on the Stuart Highway in June. (ABC News: James Elton)

Police now say they arrested a 16-year-old boy — alleged to be the driver of the vehicle at the time of the crash — on Friday.

They have charged him with driving a motor vehicle causing death, careless driving causing death, and five counts of recklessly endangering life.

He was also charged with two counts of driving a motor vehicle without consent, and one count each of driving a motor vehicle in a dangerous manner, aggravated burglary and driving never licensed.

Police say the 16-year-old has been remanded in custody and will appear in court on Monday.

Investigations into the incident are continuing and anyone with information is urged to contact police on 131 444 and quote reference NTP2600053060.

World.title: Emotional day as East Kimberley native title recognised
World.content:
It was an emotional day for traditional owners on Nganjuwarr country when the Federal Court formally recognised their native title claim to over 900 square kilometres of land and waters in northern Western Australia.

Lucilla Martin was one of about 100 traditional owners who gathered at Pelican's Nest on the Dunham River for Wednesday's on-country hearing.

"I feel so great that I want to jump over this moon, wherever it is, to be free and to do my things," she said.

But the "long journey" to formal recognition was bittersweet.

"Today I had tears for my dad, my sister, my brother and my mum, I had a bit of sadness today," Ms Martin said, reflecting on family members who had passed away.

Lucilla Martin was delighted to see the native title recognised. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

A major milestone

The Nganjuwarr native title claim filed in 2024 area covers 960 kilometres of the East Kimberley.

On Wednesday Federal Court Justice Erin Longbottom awarded claimants exclusive rights over that area, bringing the total native title coverage of the Kimberley to 97 per cent.

The hearing opened with a smoking ceremony. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

Kimberley Land Council, which represented the claim group, said the recognition put traditional owners in a stronger negotiating position with Giliwinggin Aboriginal Corporation, now appointed as the prescribed body corporate.

"It gives us an opportunity to have our voices heard and strengthens our rights and interests," deputy chief executive Sarah Parriman said.

"If effectively should mean that the government and other interested parties need to come and talk to traditional owners."

Erin Longbottom congratulates the traditional owners. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

A formal framework for resources

One of those interested parties is minerals company Tivan Limited, which is seeking approval to expand its groundwater extraction for its Speewah Project, the largest mining venture on Nganjuwarr country.

Grant Wilson and Raphael Sampi shaking hands at the event. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

Executive chairman Grant Wilson welcomed Wednesday's decision, which he said would build on the company's existing partnership with Nganjuwarr traditional owners and the Kimberley Land Council.

"The agreement we entered into at the start still governs our process. In parallel, we've been working towards what's known as an Indigenous Land Use Agreement, and that negotiation is ongoing, expected to conclude in the second half of this year," he said.

"And now we have a negotiating party that's formally recognised as having exclusive possession of native title."

Traditional owner Raphael Sampi said mining could "make our country look ugly", but was keen to engage in talks with Tivan.

"I'm going to talk up for the country, find out what they are doing … whatever they are doing, I'm going to be the one there, talking to them," he said.

World.title: Playing one of the hardest pieces of music, this 13-year-old took the music world by storm
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life Playing one of the hardest pieces of music, this 13-year-old took the music world by storm Carolyn Webb July 26, 2026 — 1:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Charlie Wu returned to school last week, he had an incredible yarn to tell his classmates about what he’d been up to during the holidays. While other kids rode bikes and played video games over their winter breaks, 13-year-old Charlie travelled to the other side of the world to compete in one of the world’s top junior piano competitions – and won. Good to be back home: Charlie Wu practising at his home in Wheelers Hill, Melbourne. Justin McManus In his final performance for the Grand Piano Competition in Russia, Charlie conquered what is known as the Mount Everest of piano pieces, Rachmaninoff’s Concerto No. 3, accompanied by the Moscow Philharmonic Orchestra. His mother, Ashleigh Wu, said she was proud and excited to witness Charlie’s triumph at Moscow’s Tchaikovsky Concert Hall, where he came equal first with Russian 10-year-old, Emir Zakaria.



“I think all his hard work paid off,” Ashleigh said. Charlie admitted that he was nervous at first, but took a deep breath and immersed himself in the music. Loading “I tried to play my heart out,” he said. Charlie began learning piano at age six; within a year, he had progressed to playing pieces by Beethoven – a strong sign of his potential and innate talent.



His piano teacher, Glenn Riddle, a Melbourne Conservatorium of Music senior lecturer, said he was “thrilled to bits” with Charlie’s win, describing the year 8 Caulfield Grammar student as a world-class pianist. “By far and away, I think he’s the most outstanding talent I’ve ever seen in Australia. No question,” Riddle said. Charlie Wu aged six, around the time he started learning piano. Ashleigh Wu Riddle, who also travelled to Moscow for the competition, described Charlie’s chosen piece of music as “virtuosic”, saying “the technical skills needed to play it are extraordinarily demanding”. In the 1996 movie Shine, based on the true story of Australian pianist David Helfgott, playing “Rach 3”, as Rachmaninoff’s Concerto No. 3 is also known, triggers his mental breakdown.



“The second movement is very brooding, lyrical and intense,” Riddle explained. “And for the final movement, imagine the most thrilling carnival ride you’ve been on at Luna Park … it’s like that from go to woah, it’s like one giant rollercoaster ride. You barely get a chance to breathe.” In addition to Charlie’s technical precision throughout his performance, Riddle said the 13-year-old showed engagement with the music and was able to communicate his passion for it to the audience. Charlie’s teacher Glenn Riddle, Charlie Wu and Charlie’s mother Ashleigh Wu outside the Bolshoi Theatre in Moscow. Ashleigh Wu “To keep the audience on the edge of their seats for an entire 25- or 30-minute concerto – that’s something very special,” he said. “And he was playing what’s often not only regarded as being the hardest, but also the most passionate concerto in the piano repertoire.”



In response to the June 19 performance, the audience “went wild for him”, Riddle said. “They called him back for three encores. A lady burst out of the audience and presented him with flowers.” Though the winning prize was a baby grand piano, Australia was deemed too far to ship such an item. Triumphant teen: Charlie Wu at his June 18 final competition performance. Instead, and on top of the cash prize of 400,000 Russian roubles ($7273), Charlie was given a cash prize of €17,000 ($27,000). But for Charlie, simply travelling to Russia and being able to play with the Moscow Philharmonic Orchestra on “one of the greatest stages in the world” was prize enough. Winning the grand prix, he said, “was an excellent bonus”. Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy. Sign up to receive our Evening Edition newsletter.

World.title: NSW man sentenced over ‘depraved’ abuse of stepdaughter
World.content:
NationalNSWCourts NSW man sentenced over ‘depraved’ abuse of stepdaughter Amber Schultz July 26, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A 45-year-old man has been sentenced to 26 years in prison for the “extreme”, “depraved” and “derogatory” sexual abuse of his teenage stepdaughter spanning three years. In his sentencing, Judge William Fitzsimmons noted the offending constituted “the most profound abuse of trust”, targeting a child he had been a father figure to since she was just three years old, and a girl he was 25 years older than. The stepfather stored hard drives with child abuse material in the ceiling of the family home. Matt Willis The offending involved “persistent”, “repeated and unrelenting abuse of a young girl” which became “increasingly depraved” and degrading as the years progressed, Fitzsimmons found. “The offender target[ed] her vulnerabilities and [there was] a significant power imbalance in the victim being overborne by the offender’s position of authority,” Fitzsimmons wrote.



The abuse began in 2021 when the girl was 15 years old, with the man helping the girl take photos for Instagram to improve her confidence and body image. It quickly escalated with the stepfather directing the girl to model in increasingly sexualised poses and outfits and taking over 1000 photos, before escalating to aggravated sexual intercourse. The abuse mostly occurred in the family home in the Illawarra region, south of Sydney, where “the victim was entitled to feel safe,” Fitzsimmons noted. The court heard the man had groomed the girl, exploited her at a vulnerable time of her life, and treated her as an object, giving her “cold and uncaring” instructions to keep the abuse secret, including from his wife, the girl’s mother. He logged every instance of the abuse in a spreadsheet, showing the child a list of his offending. In September 2024, the victim, then 18, disclosed the abuse to a friend at school. The principal and the victim’s mother were notified, and the victim reported the abuse to police. Police raided the family home, finding four external hard drives hidden in the garage roof under the insulation containing child abuse material.



The police also found videos of the man perpetrating the abuse against his stepdaughter in a hidden folder of his secret phone. He was arrested that day and has been in custody since. The man denied having a sexual attraction to children. In her victim impact statement, the young woman detailed how the abuse had impacted every aspect of her life, including her education, sense of self-worth and her relationships with others, as well as her relationship with her mother during the years of abuse. The woman said she struggled with trusting others, leading to decreased empathy and kindness, and that she no longer believed in second chances or forgiveness. “Because of every single thing I went through, I wake up a stronger person, but I’m also still that terrified 15-year-old girl crying in her room, terrified for her own safety,” she wrote.



The man pleaded guilty to 17 offences, including three counts of aggravated sexual intercourse with a child, eight counts of sexual intercourse with a child under care, child abuse production and possession charges and other sexual offences against the girl. He was given a 25 per cent discount on his sentence for his early guilty plea, and will be eligible for parole in September 2041. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. World.title: ‘Surprised and overjoyed’: Coastal community beats corporate giant to protect their beloved river
World.content:
NationalVictoriaEnvironmental protection ‘Surprised and overjoyed’: Coastal community beats corporate giant to protect their beloved river Benjamin Preiss July 26, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It was the David vs Goliath battle that stunned even the true believers when the decision landed unexpectedly in their favour. For years, residents have sounded the alarm about the terrible state of the Anglesea River. Fish kills, high acidity levels and low flows from tributaries had devastated their beloved waterway, which runs through one of Victoria’s most popular holiday spots. The former coal mine in Anglesea. Jason South The Friends of Anglesea River attributed much of the waterway’s woes to aluminium giant Alcoa’s historic practice of pumping underground water to operate its now defunct power station. The company had operated the power station for almost 50 years in Anglesea until it ceased operations in the coastal town in 2015, leaving behind a gaping pit where they used to mine coal to generate electricity.



Recently, Alcoa applied for a licence to resume pumping groundwater to fill the pit in the forested hills behind Anglesea. But earlier this month, Southern Rural Water rejected that application. Anglesea residents, including Keith Shipton, were thrilled. They had argued against granting the licence for Alcoa amid fears of further environmental damage. Shipton, the Friends of Anglesea River co-founder, said even though his group was confident its argument was backed by science, they had grown increasingly pessimistic about whether the decision would come down in their favour. Or so soon. Issy Mildenhall, Dick O’Hanlon and Keith Shipton were among the Anglesea residents celebrating the win against Alcoa. Jason South They had believed the decision might come after the state election in November.



“We were both surprised and overjoyed,” Shipton said. Group members launched Freedom of Information requests, a publicity campaign and written submissions in the hope of defeating Alcoa’s licence application. Since 2015 there have been periods of regeneration in the Anglesea River, including in October 2022 when extended heavy rain flushed it out and allowed seawater to flow back in. The fish kill in the Anglesea River last year. Justin McManus “It was just breathtaking how quickly the whole system recovered,” Shipton said. “The seagrass started growing back, and the fish were thriving.”



But mostly, the river has been in poor health over at least the past decade. “The creeks should be green veins through the catchment,” Shipton said. “They’re dead.” Melbourne University environmental geochemistry professor Ralf Haese said it was likely that acidic conditions and low flows in the Anglesea River and surrounding creeks had resulted from Alcoa’s pumping of groundwater. He said it was little surprise Alcoa’s application was rejected. The Anglesea River last year. Justin McManus “It’s the right decision,” he said.



Haese, who has done research on behalf of the Friends of Anglesea River, said pumping groundwater had lowered groundwater levels and increased acidity in the waterways. The pumping had also altered the state of the waterways, he said. “The wetlands around the creeks and rivers are drying up.” Haese said it might take decades for the pit to fill without intervention. But he said acidity levels would currently be so high that swimming in the lake posed a health risk and wildlife was unable to grow in the water. However, he said the water could be improved through treatment. The demolition by explosives of the Alcoa’s Anglesea power station in 2018. Joe Armao Alcoa ran the power station at Anglesea for 46 years until it closed permanently in 2015. Friends of Anglesea River co-founder and former Alcoa employee Dick O’Hanlon said the company previously released treated water into the Anglesea River.



Related Article Environmental protection What’s killing all the fish in this coastal town? Locals think they know He said the company used to pump four megalitres of water into the river every day. But O’Hanlon said this meant the full extent of low flows only became apparent later. “It masked the severity of the problem, although not deliberately,” he said. The most recent mass fish kill in the Anglesea River occurred last year. The Friends of Anglesea River attributed the fish deaths to the damage that was previously done to the environment, but the company argued it was part of a natural process. O’Hanlon said Alcoa’s decades of groundwater use had resulted in long-term consequences for the Anglesea River.



“The river now is dead, and it has been since last August.” Alcoa, however, disputes these suggestions about the effect of its operations on the environment. Alcoa had applied to extract 1500 megalitres of water from underground over 10 years as part of its plan to rehabilitate the gaping pit and surrounding area. But Southern Rural Water ultimately determined the proposed licence would probably result in small but potentially significant reductions in groundwater levels and river flows. In a statement, Southern Rural Water managing director Scott Cornish said the pit was expected to fill itself naturally – possibly within 26 years. It would take about 18 gigalitres of water to fill the pit. By contrast, in 2015 the ABC reported the MCG could hold 1.574 gigalitres of water.



An Alcoa spokesman said its application followed more than four years of detailed technical assessment by experienced consultants. He said that analysis concluded the proposed groundwater use would not impact the environment, including the Anglesea River. “The analysis identified that Alcoa’s past groundwater extraction has not had any significant impact on acid generation levels in surface water, and we are therefore not clear on what led to this reasoning,” he said. Anglesea is among the most popular holiday destinations in Victoria. Scott McNaughton The spokesman said allowing the pit to fill naturally would take many years and did not support the “timely outcomes” the community and government expected to ensure the site was a safe, stable and sustainable landform. The company will now determine its next steps, including whether to appeal, which it must do within 28 days of the decision in the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal. World.title: This Christian church has banned women elders. It’s a dangerous move
World.content:
NationalGender equality Opinion This Christian church has banned women elders. It’s a dangerous move Kylie Maddox Pidgeon Psychologist July 26, 2026 — 1:30pm

July 26, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The setting could hardly have been more symbolic. Last week’s general assembly of the Presbyterian Church of NSW and the ACT met in the Audrey Keown Theatre at Presbyterian Ladies’ College, Sydney, a school that has spent more than 140 years educating girls for lives of leadership. Inside those walls, an assembly that was roughly 90 per cent male voted 136-61 to ensure that women could no longer hold one of the church’s highest local leadership offices: elder. Illustration by Matt Davidson. Few venues would better expose the contradiction. PLC has a proud history of producing women who have helped shape Australian society, including Justice Carolyn Simpson, appointed to the Supreme Court of NSW, and Professor Susan Dorsch, the first woman appointed to a professorship in the University of Sydney’s faculty of medicine.



Related Article Opinion

Domestic violence The church stripped bare: high rate of domestic abuse among Anglicans exposed Julia Baird Journalist, broadcaster, historian and author Yet within the PLC theatre, the Presbyterian assembly voted that women were biblically unqualified to govern the very institution that helped educate them. Supporters describe the motion and the result as an expression of complementarianism: the theological belief that men and women are equal in worth but assigned different God-given roles within the church and family. This language is carefully chosen. “Different roles” sounds reassuringly even-handed. In practice, the distribution of power is anything but. Governance, doctrinal oversight and pastoral leadership remain reserved exclusively for men. George Orwell recognised this kind of linguistic sleight of hand. In Animal Farm, the promise from the ruling pigs that “all animals are equal” quickly gives way to the revealing qualification: “but some animals are more equal than others”. Equality, once modified, has an uncanny habit of becoming hierarchy. Research consistently shows that homogeneous leadership groups are more vulnerable to groupthink and blind spots, while diverse leadership teams tend to make stronger governance decisions, particularly when addressing complex issues.



Related Article Exclusive

Investigations God, Christ, man, woman: The ‘divine order’ that defines life for Exclusive Brethren women Advocates, researchers, royal commissions and church-commissioned reviews have repeatedly warned that gender-imbalanced leadership structures and cultures can undermine organisations’ ability to recognise, respond to and prevent domestic and family violence. An analysis published by ABC News highlighted how insular evangelical and complementarian structures frequently pressure women to remain in violent marriages under the guise of honouring God or keeping their wedding vows. Given that there is an alternative theological position of egalitarianism, it begs the question: why would Presbyterians choose the option of poorer governance that creates greater risk for women? Nina Funnell, an investigative journalist and PLC alumna, is the founder of the #LetHerSpeak campaign that has led to multiple law reforms, dismantling archaic victim-survivor “gag laws”. A Walkley and Australian Human Rights Commission Award winner, Funnell has reported extensively on gender, power and violence against women. She has worked closely with Our Watch, a national independent organisation that leads primary prevention of violence against women.



Related Article Hillsong Church When Elise finally reported her abuser to Hillsong, she was threatened and told to ‘forgive’ him Our Watch lists both “gender inequality” and “men’s control of decision-making and limits to women’s independence in public and private life” as primary drivers of men’s violence against women. Both drivers are strengthened by the assembly’s vote. Research from the Australian National University found that religious identity and participation were associated with more patriarchal beliefs about gender roles and that, while religious individuals acknowledged domestic violence was an important national issue, they did not “recognise it as an issue among members of their own faith”, Professor Naomi Priest, the study’s lead author, said. The study recommends that “addressing patriarchal beliefs and acknowledgment of domestic violence within faith communities are key targets for action to address domestic violence”. It would be comforting to imagine the assembly simply hadn’t considered the abusive implications, or more comforting still that its gathering was a dystopian fiction performed on the PLC stage. Those explanations, however, remain imaginary. The assembly had consulted widely in recent years and had received ample feedback that this decision would cause women to be less safe in their congregations. Additionally, a recent internal report presented to the assembly by its own women’s ministry committee revealed deep fractures within the wider ranks on this very issue. The committee surveyed ministers, elders and congregants in the church and found significant differences between the responses of female congregation members and male ministers to the following two statements: “Men and women work well together in this church” and “Women trust the elders in this church with issues specifically related to women (e.g. domestic violence, sexism).”



The assembly may have been more fittingly held in Orwell’s Nineteen Eighty-Four than at PLC. The doublethink going on within parts of the Presbyterian church is astonishing: declaring that women are equal to men, while the men actively restrict women’s equal voice and opportunity; claiming to abhor all forms of violence, while voting in favour of measures and structures that drive men’s violence against women; and claiming to strengthen healthy biblical relationships between men and women, while simultaneously committing acts of overt sexism and undermining the health and safety of women. The Audrey Keown Theatre exists to celebrate young women and the leaders they can become. Last week it hosted an overwhelmingly male assembly who decided precisely where to install the stained-glass ceiling. Kylie Maddox Pidgeon is a psychologist with tertiary qualifications in theology. She is a former member of the Presbyterian Church. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: No sex, please – we’re Gen Z. But this zero-eros movie neuters Homer’s Odyssey
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaCinema Opinion No sex, please – we’re Gen Z. But this zero-eros movie neuters Homer’s Odyssey Maureen Dowd New York Times columnist July 26, 2026 — 1:30pm

July 26, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Medievalists must be jealous. Classicists are having a moment on social media, happily discussing whether Odysseus was “polytropos,” “polymetis” or “polymechanos”. And that’s very cool. Thank you, Mr Nolan. Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey is a throwback to the days when Hollywood big shots fearlessly took on literary classics, undaunted by the challenges of bringing vast, thorny tales to the screen. Conjuring the Civil War in Gone With The Wind? Re-creating the desert battlefields of World War I in Lawrence of Arabia? Depicting the Russian Revolution in Doctor Zhivago? Why not? Matt Damon as Odysseus and Zendaya as his protector, the Greek goddess Athena. In the poem, Athena asks Zeus to intervene to make Calypso give up Odysseus, her sex slave. That is removed from the film. Nolan’s portal to ancient Greece has lured audiences back to theatres and spiked book sales of Homer’s The Odyssey, over 12,000 lines of dactylic hexameter verse composed in the seventh or eighth century BCE. Nolan has turned one of the foundational works of Western literature into an entertaining adventure saga.



Nolan told Stephen Colbert that he used every trick in the book to achieve his stunning visual effects. (The Mediterranean was ready for its close-up!) Yet the director failed to capture the essence of the man of tricks and twists, Odysseus, who delighted in storytelling and feigned identities. In keeping with Generation Z’s waning interest in sex, the poem’s famous sex scenes have been excised. Much of the moral ambiguity has been drained to make Matt Damon’s protagonist more likable. Except for a few mournful appearances by Zendaya’s Athena, who seems more like Odysseus’ conscience than his shape-shifting partner in deception, Nolan doesn’t depict any of the major meddling gods from the story. Besides being rich, fascinating characters, the gods are the framework for everything that happened in the ancient world. If you take the gods out of the picture, you just have people struggling within themselves. You lose the depth and force of the epic. Nolan’s nearly three-hour masterwork, classicist Mary Beard noted, does not have Homer’s “elusive sexiness”. In keeping with Generation Z’s waning interest in sex, the poem’s famous sex scenes have been excised, sapping erotic power from the female characters. As a headline in New York magazine wondered, “Is no one horny in The Odyssey?” Nolan brought the dark spirit of his last hit, Oppenheimer, with him to Greece, imbuing Odysseus with shame about his brilliant engineering invention that won the war: the horse that tricked the Trojans. His Odysseus is filled with remorse and haunted by the idea that his actions may lead to the end of civilisation as they know it.



Homer’s guy, not so much. After Odysseus and his men sacked Troy, they went across the way and sacked another city. Emily Wilson, whose popular modern translation of The Odyssey inspired Nolan, said the director turned Odysseus into an all-American hero weighed down by anxieties foreign to the ancient Greeks. “He’s traumatised Jason Bourne,” she said of Damon’s portrayal on Derek Thompson’s podcast. “He’s an action hero who feels bad about being an action hero. He’s not that complicated. Unfortunately, he’s not The Talented Mr. Ripley in this film. The Odysseus of the Greek poem is complicated.” Much of the moral ambiguity has been drained to make Matt Damon’s protagonist more likable. Nolan did not want his Odysseus betraying Penelope and enjoying his sojourns with other women. The director completely cut out the young princess Nausicaa, whom Homer’s Odysseus has a flirtation with, and neuters the text’s sexual encounters with Circe and Calypso. In Homer, Odysseus sails to Aeaea, the island home of the enchanting sorceress Circe, “the nymph with the lovely braids”. (I named my kitten after that Circe.) When Circe drugs Odysseus’ crew and taps the men with her wand, turning them into swine, it’s witchy foreplay.



The messenger god, Hermes, also a trickster, comes down from Olympus to give Odysseus an antidote for when Circe tries to use her magic on him. Hermes also advises Odysseus: “Don’t refuse the goddess’s bed,” because that’s really what Circe wants in return for turning the swine back to men. Under no spell, Odysseus says in Homer’s version, “I mounted Circe’s gorgeous bed.” He was so smitten with “the lustrous goddess” who doted on him with “sides of meat and drafts of heady wine” that he didn’t leave for a year – despite pleas from his homesick men. Nolan’s Circe, played by Samantha Morton, is like a vindictive feminist hippie making ceramic pots in Vermont, except she’s sculpting pigs. Her romance with Odysseus is scrubbed. Nolan whitewashes Odysseus’ infidelity with Calypso, played by Charlize Theron, pictured here at the world premiere of The Odyssey in London this month. Eamonn M. McCormack In Homer, Odysseus lands on the island of another luminous goddess, Calypso, and stays seven years. He’s imprisoned, but at the beginning at least, he enjoyed himself, even as Penelope was fending off boorish suitors back home. Nolan whitewashes Odysseus’ infidelity here by turning Calypso – played by Charlize Theron – into a fashionable beach therapist who gives him mood-altering lotus flowers to help with his PTSD. In Homer, Odysseus has no need to forget. He cries once over the human cost of the war when he hears a song about Troy’s fall, but mostly he’s proud of his war exploits. And the “scalawag”, as Calypso calls him, doesn’t partake of the lotus; his men become addicted lotus-eaters on a different island. In the movie, Calypso graciously lets Odysseus go when he comes out of his lotus fog and insists on returning home. In the book, Athena has to ask Zeus to intervene to make Calypso give up her sex slave, and she complains that there’s a double standard, because the male gods have affairs with mortals but interfere when the female gods are similarly romping. Penelope, a mortal, is expected to be faithful, no matter that Odysseus’ sexual liaisons have added eight years to his 10-year voyage home.



When Homer’s Odysseus finally gets home, there’s a charged scene where he is outraged to see that the marital bed he built, crafted out of an olive tree that grew inside the palace, has been moved. It’s a test by Penelope. Nolan dispensed with that, too. Related Article Opinion

Work/life balance Odysseus didn’t rest on his laurels. But like the rest of us, maybe he should have Julia Baird Journalist, broadcaster, historian and author The director also sanitised Odysseus’ character by skipping the scene near the end when the hero orders his son to round up the 12 female servants who slept with suitors and hack them to death with a sword. Telemachus convinces his father that the women should be hanged instead. Nolan’s IMAX Odysseus gives up the crown for his son and goes into exile with Penelope to redeem his actions during the war. Homer’s hero? No way! Homer did not portray a world turning against violence. He limned a profoundly martial universe interspersed with lots of magic and sex and cavorting, conniving immortals. If you smooth it out and modernise it too much, you lose what made it so important to begin with. And you’re just left with a guy finding his way home.

World.title: India’s ‘cockroach’ protesters claim surprise victory as government accepts their demands
World.content:
WorldAsiaProtests India’s ‘cockroach’ protesters claim surprise victory as government accepts their demands Saurabh Sharma , Aftab Ahmed and Shilpa Jamkhandikar July 26, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New Delhi: Indian youth protesters have called off weeks of demonstrations and celebrated in the streets after the education minister quit and Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government bowed to demands including calls to fix a cheating-prone exam system. The worst political crisis of Modi’s third term in office had peaked this week when thousands of protesters marched on parliament, with police using tear gas to control them. Young voters form a critical base of his Bharatiya Janata Party. But youths calling themselves “cockroaches” had taken to the streets since late June, after national exam papers were leaked, forcing a resit that affected 2 million students and galvanising anger about the lack of prospects for young Indians. Supporters of India’s Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) celebrate following the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. Getty Images The resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, the students’ primary demand, came as a surprise because Modi has a reputation for refusing to act under pressure.



Modi’s party faces key state elections next year. Similar youth-led protest movements brought down governments in neighbouring Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bangladesh in recent years. Related Article Opinion

India Young people are revolting. India’s ‘cockroach’ campaign is just the latest example Peter Hartcher Political and international editor Celebrations erupted at the Jantar Mantar protest site in the capital Delhi, with thousands of youngsters chanting victory slogans and dancing. The youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) movement, which spearheaded the demonstrations, said it would end its protests. “We have done it,” said Abhijeet Dipke, CJP’s founder, to loud cheers at the site.



Youngsters shouted “Jai Hind”, a patriotic slogan meaning “Victory to India”, as the national anthem played on loudspeakers and sweets were distributed. Roads around the central business district of Connaught Place, near the protest site, were shut amid celebrations and a swelling crowd of thousands of protesters. Celebrations erupted in Delhi, with thousands of youngsters chanting victory slogans and dancing. Getty Images Health Minister J.P. Nadda and Jitendra Singh, a junior minister in Modi’s office, held a joint press conference with two CJP spokespersons after another round of talks following Pradhan’s resignation. Nadda said the government had accepted all demands of the protesters, which included reforms in the exam system, dropping police cases filed against protesters and compensating families of students who died by suicide after the exam paper leaks.



“The Cockroach Janta Party declares that we withdraw the agitation in good faith,” CJP spokesperson Saurav Das said. “All the demands raised by our team have been accepted; therefore we request protesters to withdraw and peacefully go home,” spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka added. Young people calling themselves “cockroaches” have taken to the streets since late June after national exam papers were leaked. AP “The bottom line is we have won, your struggle, hard work, and patience have paid off,” Ranka told cheering crowds at Jantar Mantar on returning from the talks, and urged them to withdraw peacefully. Opposition parties had echoed the demands of the youth and disrupted the monsoon session of parliament for the entire week, threatening key legislation planned by the government.



Scenes of police using tear gas to control protesters had also fuelled public anger, although authorities defended their actions, saying they were only enforcing the law. Pradhan announced his resignation in a post on X. Supporters of the Cockroach Janta Party scuffling with police last week. AP Photo/Vipin “Considering the situation that has arisen at Jantar Mantar and across the country, so that anti-national forces do not take advantage of this situation ... I have sent my resignation letter to the prime minister,” Pradhan wrote. “I deeply respect the aspirations, feelings, and legitimate expectations of the country’s youth.”



The protesters had demanded his resignation over leaks of the national medical school entrance test paper in May, which led to the cancellation of results and a re-test that affected 2 million students. The protests also reflected growing anger in India over job scarcity and government accountability. Pradhan’s resignation is “a victory of peace, patience & perseverance”, activist Sonam Wangchuk, who was on a hunger strike for 26 days to support the youth movement, wrote on X. After news of his resignation, federal authorities restored access to the mobile internet around the protest site after blocking it for most of the week. Delhi Metro rail stations in and around the area that were closed across four days this week were also opened.



“Young generation is here. This is a win for the constitution,” protester Tluanga Ralte said, walking with a copy of the Indian constitution at the protest site after Pradhan’s resignation. “We are not a lazy generation.” Editor's pick China relations Chickens, Chairman Mao and spiced tea with the neighbours: Welcome to ‘the real China’ Pradhan, 57, a senior member of Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party and the son of a veteran BJP leader, had been education minister since 2021. Pradhan, who in the past was mentioned as a potential BJP president, is only the second minister to resign following a scandal since Modi came to power in 2014. M.J. Akbar resigned as junior foreign minister in October 2018 to fight allegations of sexual harassment made by more than a dozen women during India’s #MeToo movement.

World.title: Horse owner vindicated after two-year battle with Olympic sport
World.content:
SportEquestrian Horse owner vindicated after two-year battle with Olympic sport Chris Barrett July 26, 2026 — 12:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A tribunal has ruled against national federation Equestrian Australia (EA) after a nearly two-year dispute over one of the Olympic sport’s most coveted prizes. The feud centred around the scoring system used at the 2024 Australian Dressage Championships at the Sydney International Equestrian Centre and divided officials in the exclusive sport. Vivien Lipshut with her horse Estupendo, which no longer competes in dressage. Paul Jeffers The taxpayer-funded peak body fought claims by Victorian horse owner Vivien Lipshut that her imported European gelding Estupendo and his rider David McKinnon were wrongly denied the title of Australian grand prix champion. However, the National Sports Tribunal has found against EA, determining Estupendo and McKinnon the rightful winners after hearing that the scoring format was changed without the knowledge of entrants in the days before the event.



Lipshut alleged she had faced intimidation from one of the sport’s former integrity officers during her bid to have the original result reversed and was vindicated by the decision of tribunal member Anthony Lo Surdo SC. “This was never just about winning a championship. It was about standing up for fairness, accountability, and the integrity of our sport,” Lipshut said. David McKinnon rides Estupendo at the Australian Dressage Championships at Sydney International Equestrian Centre in 2024. Simon Scully “I could not stand by and allow an injustice like this to go unchallenged. If the rules can be ignored in one case, they can be ignored in any case. Every member deserves to know that the rules will be applied fairly and consistently, regardless of who is involved.” Six-time Olympian Mary Hanna and her Paris 2024 reserve horse Ivanhoe 1 were declared the victors after the Australian championships two years ago under on a points system applied by Dressage NSW event organiser Toni Venhaus in the lead-up to competition after consultation with the EA’s Dressage Committee.



But the tribunal determined the scoring change was invalid and against EA’s own rules, concluding that the grand prix champion should have been calculated with the percentage-based model typically deployed in dressage, where horses are judged on their movements during a routine. On that basis, Estupendo and McKinnon would have had the edge. Reacting to the tribunal’s ruling, state organisations Equestrian NSW and Dressage NSW said the championship rug for 2024 would be presented again next month at their awards night. “The decision provides important clarity regarding the application of the rules and reinforces the importance of fairness, consistency and transparency across our sport,” they said. “We extend our sincere congratulations to Viv Lipshut, David McKinnon and Estupendo on being recognised as the 2024 Australian grand prix champion. This is a significant achievement and one that deserves to be celebrated.”



Lipshut, who herself stopped riding after having a stroke in 2017, has accepted an invitation to attend the NSW awards dinner. Related Article Investigation

Equestrian Scoring feud, intimidation claim engulfs Olympics’ most expensive sport But after encountering resistance from national-level officials from the moment she questioned the outcome of the blue riband event, she said the battle had taken its toll. EA opposed the matter being sent to the Australian government’s independent sports umpire, but the tribunal accepted it after an investigation by this masthead. “Although I am grateful this matter has now been resolved, the nearly two-year struggle has come at a considerable personal cost to my health and wellbeing,” Lipshut said.



“My sincere hope is that this determination will help ensure that no member of Equestrian Australia ever has to endure such a prolonged struggle again simply to have their concerns heard.” Equestrian Australia, which will receive $5.7 million in federal funding in 2026-27 via the Australian Sports Commission, has also been embroiled in a legal dispute with its former digital services provider. It has vowed to vigorously defend separate proceedings brought against it by former Olympian Heath Ryan in the NSW Supreme Court. Ryan’s EA membership has been provisionally suspended for more than a year while the International Federation for Equestrian Sports investigates a video that showed him whipping a horse 42 times. World.title: Playing one of the hardest pieces of music, this 13-year-old took the music world by storm
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life Playing one of the hardest pieces of music, this 13-year-old took the music world by storm Carolyn Webb July 26, 2026 — 1:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Charlie Wu returned to school last week, he had an incredible yarn to tell his classmates about what he’d been up to during the holidays. While other kids rode bikes and played video games over their winter breaks, 13-year-old Charlie travelled to the other side of the world to compete in one of the world’s top junior piano competitions – and won. Good to be back home: Charlie Wu practising at his home in Wheelers Hill, Melbourne. Justin McManus In his final performance for the Grand Piano Competition in Russia, Charlie conquered what is known as the Mount Everest of piano pieces, Rachmaninoff’s Concerto No. 3, accompanied by the Moscow Philharmonic Orchestra. His mother, Ashleigh Wu, said she was proud and excited to witness Charlie’s triumph at Moscow’s Tchaikovsky Concert Hall, where he came equal first with Russian 10-year-old, Emir Zakaria.



“I think all his hard work paid off,” Ashleigh said. Charlie admitted that he was nervous at first, but took a deep breath and immersed himself in the music. Loading “I tried to play my heart out,” he said. Charlie began learning piano at age six; within a year, he had progressed to playing pieces by Beethoven – a strong sign of his potential and innate talent.



His piano teacher, Glenn Riddle, a Melbourne Conservatorium of Music senior lecturer, said he was “thrilled to bits” with Charlie’s win, describing the year 8 Caulfield Grammar student as a world-class pianist. “By far and away, I think he’s the most outstanding talent I’ve ever seen in Australia. No question,” Riddle said. Charlie Wu aged six, around the time he started learning piano. Ashleigh Wu Riddle, who also travelled to Moscow for the competition, described Charlie’s chosen piece of music as “virtuosic”, saying “the technical skills needed to play it are extraordinarily demanding”. In the 1996 movie Shine, based on the true story of Australian pianist David Helfgott, playing “Rach 3”, as Rachmaninoff’s Concerto No. 3 is also known, triggers his mental breakdown.



“The second movement is very brooding, lyrical and intense,” Riddle explained. “And for the final movement, imagine the most thrilling carnival ride you’ve been on at Luna Park … it’s like that from go to woah, it’s like one giant rollercoaster ride. You barely get a chance to breathe.” In addition to Charlie’s technical precision throughout his performance, Riddle said the 13-year-old showed engagement with the music and was able to communicate his passion for it to the audience. Charlie’s teacher Glenn Riddle, Charlie Wu and Charlie’s mother Ashleigh Wu outside the Bolshoi Theatre in Moscow. Ashleigh Wu “To keep the audience on the edge of their seats for an entire 25- or 30-minute concerto – that’s something very special,” he said. “And he was playing what’s often not only regarded as being the hardest, but also the most passionate concerto in the piano repertoire.”



In response to the June 19 performance, the audience “went wild for him”, Riddle said. “They called him back for three encores. A lady burst out of the audience and presented him with flowers.” Though the winning prize was a baby grand piano, Australia was deemed too far to ship such an item. Triumphant teen: Charlie Wu at his June 18 final competition performance. Instead, and on top of the cash prize of 400,000 Russian roubles ($7273), Charlie was given a cash prize of €17,000 ($27,000). But for Charlie, simply travelling to Russia and being able to play with the Moscow Philharmonic Orchestra on “one of the greatest stages in the world” was prize enough. Winning the grand prix, he said, “was an excellent bonus”. Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy. Sign up to receive our Evening Edition newsletter.

World.title: NSW man sentenced over ‘depraved’ abuse of stepdaughter
World.content:
NationalNSWCourts NSW man sentenced over ‘depraved’ abuse of stepdaughter Amber Schultz July 26, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A 45-year-old man has been sentenced to 26 years in prison for the “extreme”, “depraved” and “derogatory” sexual abuse of his teenage stepdaughter spanning three years. In his sentencing, Judge William Fitzsimmons noted the offending constituted “the most profound abuse of trust”, targeting a child he had been a father figure to since she was just three years old, and a girl he was 25 years older than. The stepfather stored hard drives with child abuse material in the ceiling of the family home. Matt Willis The offending involved “persistent”, “repeated and unrelenting abuse of a young girl” which became “increasingly depraved” and degrading as the years progressed, Fitzsimmons found. “The offender target[ed] her vulnerabilities and [there was] a significant power imbalance in the victim being overborne by the offender’s position of authority,” Fitzsimmons wrote.



The abuse began in 2021 when the girl was 15 years old, with the man helping the girl take photos for Instagram to improve her confidence and body image. It quickly escalated with the stepfather directing the girl to model in increasingly sexualised poses and outfits and taking over 1000 photos, before escalating to aggravated sexual intercourse. The abuse mostly occurred in the family home in the Illawarra region, south of Sydney, where “the victim was entitled to feel safe,” Fitzsimmons noted. The court heard the man had groomed the girl, exploited her at a vulnerable time of her life, and treated her as an object, giving her “cold and uncaring” instructions to keep the abuse secret, including from his wife, the girl’s mother. He logged every instance of the abuse in a spreadsheet, showing the child a list of his offending. In September 2024, the victim, then 18, disclosed the abuse to a friend at school. The principal and the victim’s mother were notified, and the victim reported the abuse to police. Police raided the family home, finding four external hard drives hidden in the garage roof under the insulation containing child abuse material.



The police also found videos of the man perpetrating the abuse against his stepdaughter in a hidden folder of his secret phone. He was arrested that day and has been in custody since. The man denied having a sexual attraction to children. In her victim impact statement, the young woman detailed how the abuse had impacted every aspect of her life, including her education, sense of self-worth and her relationships with others, as well as her relationship with her mother during the years of abuse. The woman said she struggled with trusting others, leading to decreased empathy and kindness, and that she no longer believed in second chances or forgiveness. “Because of every single thing I went through, I wake up a stronger person, but I’m also still that terrified 15-year-old girl crying in her room, terrified for her own safety,” she wrote.



The man pleaded guilty to 17 offences, including three counts of aggravated sexual intercourse with a child, eight counts of sexual intercourse with a child under care, child abuse production and possession charges and other sexual offences against the girl. He was given a 25 per cent discount on his sentence for his early guilty plea, and will be eligible for parole in September 2041. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. World.title: ‘Surprised and overjoyed’: Coastal community beats corporate giant to protect their beloved river
World.content:
NationalVictoriaEnvironmental protection ‘Surprised and overjoyed’: Coastal community beats corporate giant to protect their beloved river Benjamin Preiss July 26, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It was the David vs Goliath battle that stunned even the true believers when the decision landed unexpectedly in their favour. For years, residents have sounded the alarm about the terrible state of the Anglesea River. Fish kills, high acidity levels and low flows from tributaries had devastated their beloved waterway, which runs through one of Victoria’s most popular holiday spots. The former coal mine in Anglesea. Jason South The Friends of Anglesea River attributed much of the waterway’s woes to aluminium giant Alcoa’s historic practice of pumping underground water to operate its now defunct power station. The company had operated the power station for almost 50 years in Anglesea until it ceased operations in the coastal town in 2015, leaving behind a gaping pit where they used to mine coal to generate electricity.



Recently, Alcoa applied for a licence to resume pumping groundwater to fill the pit in the forested hills behind Anglesea. But earlier this month, Southern Rural Water rejected that application. Anglesea residents, including Keith Shipton, were thrilled. They had argued against granting the licence for Alcoa amid fears of further environmental damage. Shipton, the Friends of Anglesea River co-founder, said even though his group was confident its argument was backed by science, they had grown increasingly pessimistic about whether the decision would come down in their favour. Or so soon. Issy Mildenhall, Dick O’Hanlon and Keith Shipton were among the Anglesea residents celebrating the win against Alcoa. Jason South They had believed the decision might come after the state election in November.



“We were both surprised and overjoyed,” Shipton said. Group members launched Freedom of Information requests, a publicity campaign and written submissions in the hope of defeating Alcoa’s licence application. Since 2015 there have been periods of regeneration in the Anglesea River, including in October 2022 when extended heavy rain flushed it out and allowed seawater to flow back in. The fish kill in the Anglesea River last year. Justin McManus “It was just breathtaking how quickly the whole system recovered,” Shipton said. “The seagrass started growing back, and the fish were thriving.”



But mostly, the river has been in poor health over at least the past decade. “The creeks should be green veins through the catchment,” Shipton said. “They’re dead.” Melbourne University environmental geochemistry professor Ralf Haese said it was likely that acidic conditions and low flows in the Anglesea River and surrounding creeks had resulted from Alcoa’s pumping of groundwater. He said it was little surprise Alcoa’s application was rejected. The Anglesea River last year. Justin McManus “It’s the right decision,” he said.



Haese, who has done research on behalf of the Friends of Anglesea River, said pumping groundwater had lowered groundwater levels and increased acidity in the waterways. The pumping had also altered the state of the waterways, he said. “The wetlands around the creeks and rivers are drying up.” Haese said it might take decades for the pit to fill without intervention. But he said acidity levels would currently be so high that swimming in the lake posed a health risk and wildlife was unable to grow in the water. However, he said the water could be improved through treatment. The demolition by explosives of the Alcoa’s Anglesea power station in 2018. Joe Armao Alcoa ran the power station at Anglesea for 46 years until it closed permanently in 2015. Friends of Anglesea River co-founder and former Alcoa employee Dick O’Hanlon said the company previously released treated water into the Anglesea River.



Related Article Environmental protection What’s killing all the fish in this coastal town? Locals think they know He said the company used to pump four megalitres of water into the river every day. But O’Hanlon said this meant the full extent of low flows only became apparent later. “It masked the severity of the problem, although not deliberately,” he said. The most recent mass fish kill in the Anglesea River occurred last year. The Friends of Anglesea River attributed the fish deaths to the damage that was previously done to the environment, but the company argued it was part of a natural process. O’Hanlon said Alcoa’s decades of groundwater use had resulted in long-term consequences for the Anglesea River.



“The river now is dead, and it has been since last August.” Alcoa, however, disputes these suggestions about the effect of its operations on the environment. Alcoa had applied to extract 1500 megalitres of water from underground over 10 years as part of its plan to rehabilitate the gaping pit and surrounding area. But Southern Rural Water ultimately determined the proposed licence would probably result in small but potentially significant reductions in groundwater levels and river flows. In a statement, Southern Rural Water managing director Scott Cornish said the pit was expected to fill itself naturally – possibly within 26 years. It would take about 18 gigalitres of water to fill the pit. By contrast, in 2015 the ABC reported the MCG could hold 1.574 gigalitres of water.



An Alcoa spokesman said its application followed more than four years of detailed technical assessment by experienced consultants. He said that analysis concluded the proposed groundwater use would not impact the environment, including the Anglesea River. “The analysis identified that Alcoa’s past groundwater extraction has not had any significant impact on acid generation levels in surface water, and we are therefore not clear on what led to this reasoning,” he said. Anglesea is among the most popular holiday destinations in Victoria. Scott McNaughton The spokesman said allowing the pit to fill naturally would take many years and did not support the “timely outcomes” the community and government expected to ensure the site was a safe, stable and sustainable landform. The company will now determine its next steps, including whether to appeal, which it must do within 28 days of the decision in the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal.
